## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**15.1  15.1 Basic and Simple Agricultural Tools**

- **Q1** (4 marks) A wedge is two sloping faces meeting at a thin edge, and a cutting tool works by driving that thin edge into the material so that the sloping faces force the material apart sideways. What actually does the cutting is PRESSURE - the push divided by the area it acts on. A thin blade puts the same push onto a very small area of contact, so the pressure at the edge is enormous, high enough to part the fibres cleanly. A thick blade spreads the same push over a much wider area, the pressure is far lower, and the blade crushes and tears instead of cutting - so more force is needed and the cut is ragged. That is exactly why sharpening works: it grinds metal away from behind the edge and makes the contact area small again.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: cutlass, hoe, axe, sickle, shears, machete saw, scythe, pruning saw, secateurs, chisel.
- **Q3** (3 marks) (a) A cutlass (or machete). It has a long heavy blade that will take down woody growth, and it is long enough to use without stooping. (b) A sickle. Its curved blade lets you gather a handful of stems and cut them with one pull, which is far faster than cutting them one at a time. (c) Shears for a long run of hedge, or secateurs for individual stems. Both give a clean cut that does not crush the stem, which matters because a crushed stem is left open to disease - a cutlass would bruise it.

**15.2  15.2 Importance of Proper Handling and Maintenance of Agricultural Tools**

- **Q4** (4 marks) For lifting root crops: a fork has separate tines with gaps between them, so it slides down into the soil around the roots and lifts them out with the soil falling away between the tines. The roots pass between the tines rather than being cut, so the crop comes up whole and undamaged - which matters because a cut tuber rots in storage. A spade has a solid blade that will slice straight through any root in its path. For turning a bed over, the solid blade is exactly what is wanted: it lifts a whole slice of soil and turns it over, burying weeds and working compost in thoroughly. A fork would let most of the soil dribble straight back through the gaps and would leave the bed half turned.
- **Q5** (3 marks) A dibber is a pointed stick or rod used to make a small hole at the right depth for a single seed or a seedling. An auger is a screw-shaped boring tool used to make deep, wide holes - for fence posts, or for planting trees and cassava cuttings - and it brings the loosened soil up as it turns.
- **Q6** (3 marks) He should use a hoe, or an auger if he has one. A dibber is only a pointed stick pushed in by hand; in hard dry ground it simply cannot be forced deep enough, and forcing it either bends the point or drives the seed too deep to come up. A hoe has a steel blade on a long handle, so the farmer can use leverage and his own weight to break the crust first and then open a proper hole, and an auger is designed precisely to bore into ground that a stick will not enter.

**15.3  15.3 Rules for Handling Agricultural Tools Safely**

- **Q7** (4 marks) A tool is handheld, has no moving parts of its own, and is worked directly by the user's muscles. A machine has moving parts and is driven by something other than the user's hands - an engine, a motor or a draught animal - and it usually does several operations in one pass. Hoe: a tool - one solid implement with no moving parts, worked entirely by the arms. Knapsack sprayer: a machine - it has a pump, a hose and a nozzle, moving parts that pressurise the liquid and break it into a spray; the user only works the pump. Tractor-drawn plough: a machine - the share and the mouldboard do the work and it is pulled by an engine rather than pushed by a person. Combine harvester: a machine, and the clearest case - an engine drives many moving parts and it reaps, threshes and cleans the grain in a single operation.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. It works far faster and covers a much larger area in a day, which matters where the land has to be prepared within a short planting window. It turns the soil deeper and more thoroughly, bringing fresh soil to the top and burying weeds properly. It needs far less human labour, which matters where labour is scarce or expensive, or where the household is small.
- **Q9** (3 marks) (a) A wheelbarrow. It carries a heavy load with the weight taken by the wheel, so one person can move far more than they could carry in their arms, and it tips out exactly where it is wanted. (b) A knapsack sprayer. It carries the chemical on the back and pumps it out as a fine spray, so the crop is covered evenly and far less chemical is used than if it were watered on. (c) A combine harvester. It cuts, threshes and cleans the grain in one pass, a job that would take many people many days by hand.

**15.4  15.4 Maintaining Agricultural Tools in the Community**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Rusting is the reaction of iron with oxygen and water together - it needs both, and it will not happen in dry air, nor in water with no air dissolved in it. A hoe left with wet soil stuck to it therefore has everything the reaction needs: iron, water from the soil, and air all around it. The surface turns to hydrated iron oxide, which flakes away and exposes fresh metal underneath. Drying removes the water, so the reaction cannot start. Oiling then lays a barrier over the metal so that air, and any water that later reaches it, cannot touch the iron. Drying alone does not last, because damp air and dew will wet the tool again as soon as it is put away. Oiling alone does not work on a tool that is already wet, because the water is trapped underneath the film. So it is: dry first, then oil, then store dry.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. Wash or wipe off the soil and plant sap. Dry it thoroughly. Sharpen the edge, if it is a cutting tool, working along the edge and keeping the original angle. Oil or grease the metal parts. Check that the handle is tight and not split. Store it hanging up in a dry shed rather than left on the ground.
- **Q12** (3 marks) The head should be re-seated: driven back on firmly, with the handle replaced if the wood has shrunk or split, and a wedge or a nail driven in to hold it tight. Working with a loose head is dangerous because the blade can fly off the handle in the middle of a swing. A cutlass head is heavy, sharp and travelling fast at the instant it comes free, so it can strike the user or anyone working nearby. This is the commonest avoidable accident with hand tools on the farm, and the check takes a few seconds.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) Pressure is the push divided by the area it acts on. A sharp edge is extremely thin, so the whole push is concentrated onto a line of contact only a tiny fraction of a millimetre wide; the pressure there is enormous, high enough to part the fibres of the stem cleanly with very little effort. A blunt edge is rounded, so the same push is spread over a much wider area, the pressure is far lower, and the blade crushes and tears rather than cutting - which takes far more force. The results show exactly that: the sharp blade cut with a mean of 3.2 N against 11.7 N for the blunt one, about 3.7 times less. Sharpening works precisely because it grinds metal away from behind the edge and makes that contact area small again.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Repeating and averaging guards against the fact that individual stems differ - one may be knobbly, woody, damp or dry - and against slips in reading the balance. A single reading may be high or low for a reason that has nothing to do with which blade was used; the mean of three is far more likely to reflect the blade. What must be kept the same: the same kind of stem, of the same thickness, cut at the same point along it, for both blades; and the same angle of blade to stem. Ideally the same person should do every cut, pressing at the same steady rate.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Cut away from the body and keep the other hand well clear, so that if the blade slips it travels into empty air rather than into a hand or a leg. Never press down while anyone is standing in front of or beside the rig: under 12 N of push a slipping blade travels a long way and fast. Rest the stem on a firm block instead of holding it in the hand, so the blade cannot reach the fingers. Wear closed shoes in case the blade or the block is dropped.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the question that turns 15.1 from a naming exercise into science. Every cutting tool is a wedge, and what does the work is pressure - force over area. Pupils who can say 'the sharp edge concentrates the force onto a tiny area' have understood the whole set of tools; pupils who can only list them have not. Q13 in the practical asks the same thing with numbers attached.
- Q4 on fork versus spade is the best application question here, because the answer reverses: the gaps that make a fork useless for turning a bed are exactly what make it right for lifting tubers. Look for pupils who notice that the property is the same in both cases and the job is what changes.
- Q7 on tools versus machines runs into the wheelbarrow, which is genuinely awkward - it has a wheel but no engine and does nothing by itself. I left it out of the question for that reason, but a sharp pupil may raise it; the honest answer is that it is a compound tool that uses a wheel and lever, not a machine in the sense used here.
- Q10 on rust is worth doing properly. Pupils know 'iron rusts when wet' but not that it needs oxygen AND water together, and that is why drying alone does not hold and oiling a wet tool does nothing. The five-step routine then makes sense instead of being a list to memorise.
- The cutting experiment needs a rigid frame, a spring balance reading to 0.1 N, and a blade that can be changed. Use a fresh green stem such as a cassava or hibiscus cutting of a consistent thickness, and cut several to the same gauge beforehand. Twelve newtons will overload a 10 N balance, so use a 20 N or 50 N one for the blunt blade.
- The blunt blade should be genuinely blunt - rub the edge on a stone, or use an old knife. Do not let pupils use a razor-sharp blade for this; a sharp enough edge to give 3 N will cut fingers before anyone notices.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**6.1  6.1 Types of Domestic Animals in Ghana**

- **Q1** (4 marks) An animal is domestic when people keep it, feed it, house it and control its breeding, so that it depends on people rather than fending for itself. That is a RELATIONSHIP, not a kind of animal - which is why the same species can be domestic in one place and wild in another. The caged grasscutter is fed by its keeper, protected from weather and predators, and bred from animals the keeper chose, so it is domestic. The one in the bush finds its own food and shelter, escapes its own predators and breeds with whichever partner it meets, so it is wild. Nothing about the animal's body changed - only its relationship with people did.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any two, each stated: poultry have feathers, while the others have hair or bristles; poultry have a beak and no teeth; poultry lay eggs with a hard shell rather than giving birth to live young; poultry have two legs and wings, while the others walk on four legs. Any two of these earns the marks.
- **Q3** (2 marks) Milk: cattle, goats (sheep are also correct). Meat: cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, poultry, rabbits, grasscutter - any two of these.

**6.2  6.2 Classifying Domestic Animals: Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry**

- **Q4** (3 marks) Chewing the cud means bringing food back up from the stomach into the mouth to chew it a second time, after it was first swallowed almost unchewed. It puts the animal in the ruminant group because only an animal with a four-chambered stomach can do it: the food is swallowed to the first chamber, softened there, brought back up, chewed properly, then swallowed again to pass through the rest of the chambers. A monogastric animal has one simple stomach and no way of bringing food back up, so it cannot chew the cud - which makes the behaviour a reliable test for the group.
- **Q5** (3 marks) It has hooves, so it is not poultry - the key sends poultry off on the feathers branch. It does not chew the cud, so it is not a ruminant. That leaves the 'neither' branch, so it is MONOGASTRIC. It could be a pig, a rabbit or a grasscutter - any one of those named earns the mark.

**6.3  6.3 Differences and Similarities Among Ruminants, Monogastrics and Poultry**

- **Q6** (4 marks) Grass is largely cellulose, the tough material in plant cell walls, and very few animals can break it down. The cow can, because its rumen - the biggest of the four chambers - holds huge numbers of micro-organisms that digest cellulose for it. The four chambers also give the food a long time and a great deal of space to be worked on, and chewing the cud breaks the grass into smaller pieces so the microbes can get at more of it. The pig has one simple stomach and no such chamber, so cellulose passes straight through it undigested. The pig has to be given food that is easier to break down - grains, roots, kitchen waste - instead of grass.
- **Q7** (3 marks) A newborn calf's rumen is still small and undeveloped, and the population of micro-organisms that does the digesting has not yet built up in it. So the young calf is, in effect, a monogastric animal at this stage: milk goes straight to the abomasum, the true stomach, and is digested there. Only as the calf starts eating solid feed does the rumen grow and the microbes establish themselves, and only then does the animal become a functioning ruminant able to live on grass.

**6.4  6.4 Domestic and Commercial Uses of Animals**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Draught power. Without a tractor, the farmer still has to plough, harrow and cart, and animals are the only source of pulling power available to him. A pair of oxen or a donkey lets him prepare land that he could not work by hoe, and prepare it in time for the rains, which is the difference between a crop and no crop. Draught power also comes round every season, unlike meat which can only be had once. Manure would be the second most important, because the animals feed his soil as well as pull his plough.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Meat can only be had once, at the end, and getting it means the animal is gone. While the animal is alive it gives other things repeatedly: milk or eggs every day, draught power every season, and manure every year. A living animal is also a store of wealth that can be sold in an emergency - school fees, a hospital bill, a failed harvest - which is often worth more to a household than the meat would be. So meat is the least useful of the uses for most of the animal's life, and the last one a farmer would choose.

**6.5  6.5 By-Products of Animals and Their Importance**

- **Q10** (4 marks) A by-product is a leftover of little account, and dung is not that. On a mixed farm the dung is the link that joins the two halves together: the crops feed the animal, and the animal's dung feeds the soil that grows the crops. It returns organic matter and nutrients to the ground, which keeps the soil crumbly, holds water and feeds the organisms in it. Without it the farmer would have to buy fertiliser for exactly the nutrients the animals have already produced. So the dung is what makes the farm a system rather than two separate activities - it is central to how the farm works, not a leftover from it.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Any two uses: shoes and sandals, bags and belts, drums, chairs and stools, jackets. Before it can be used a hide has to be treated - cleaned, salted or dried, and then tanned. If it is not treated it either rots, because it is protein and micro-organisms feed on it, or it dries stiff and brittle and cracks. Tanning is what turns a perishable skin into leather that lasts.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q12** (4 marks) A is the cow - it has hooves, chews the cud and has horns. B is the sheep - it has hooves and chews the cud, but has no horns. C is the pig - it has hooves but does not chew the cud. D is the fowl - it is the only one with feathers, and it has no hooves and does not chew the cud.
- **Q13** (4 marks) 'Has hooves' is YES for A, B and C at the same time, so it splits the four animals into a group of three and a group of one and then stops: it cannot tell you which of the three you have. A feature only identifies an animal if it belongs to that animal and to no other, so that following it down the table leaves exactly one possibility. 'Has horns' is YES for A alone, so it picks out the cow on its own and settles the question in a single step. That is the whole principle behind a key: each feature should cut the remaining animals into two, and keep cutting until one is left.
- **Q14** (3 marks) A goat would show no feathers, hooves YES, chews the cud YES and - for many goats - horns YES. That makes its column the same as the cow's, or the same as the sheep's, so the table can no longer separate them: two animals now share a column and the key fails. The pupil would have to add another feature that tells them apart, something like size, the shape of the horns, the coat, or the presence of a beard. The point is that a key has to be built for the animals actually in front of you, and a feature that worked for four may stop working at five.
- **Q15** (3 marks) A dichotomous key is a tool for identifying an organism by working through a series of paired statements and choosing the one that fits. Each step offers exactly two choices, and they are opposites - has feathers or does not, chews the cud or does not. That guarantees the animal must take one branch or the other and cannot fall between them, so every animal follows exactly one path through the key and arrives at exactly one name. With more than two choices at a step, or choices that overlap, an animal could take two paths and the key would give two different answers.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 78% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the question that decides whether a pupil understands 'domestic' at all. Most will define it as 'an animal that lives with people' and stop, which does not survive the grasscutter test. The point is that it is a RELATIONSHIP - kept, fed, housed, bred by people - not a kind of animal, so the same species can be either.
- Q6 on why a cow can live on grass and a pig cannot is the heart of 6.3. Pupils know the ruminant has four chambers but rarely know WHY that matters: the rumen is a fermentation vat holding micro-organisms that digest cellulose. Without that, four chambers are just a fact to memorise.
- Q7 on the newborn calf is the question I would not want to cut. It is the same idea turned round - a calf is functionally monogastric until its rumen develops - and it tests whether the pupil has understood 6.3 or only learned the diagram.
- Q10 on dung is deliberately contrary. The diagram files it under by-products, and the question asks the pupil to reject that. On a mixed farm the dung is the coupling between the animal half and the crop half; a pupil who sees that has understood farming as a system.
- Q13 is the best question in the practical. Pupils think a feature that narrows things down is useful; the insight is that a feature must be UNIQUE to identify. 'Has hooves' narrows four to three and then stops. 'Has horns' settles it in one step.
- Q14 extends that: add a goat and the key breaks, because the goat shares a column with the cow or the sheep. Good pupils will say the key has to be rebuilt for the animals actually present. This is the most transferable idea in the paper.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**19.1  19.1 What is Sustainable Energy?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular place and moment - whether it is hot, raining, windy or clear - and it can change within the hour. Climate is the average pattern of weather in a place, measured over many years, usually thirty or more. One heavy rainstorm is a single weather event: Accra has always had heavy rainstorms, and one of them tells you nothing about the average. To say the climate has changed you need the record - the total rainfall, the number of rainy days, the dates the rains began and ended, measured every year for decades and compared. If those averages have moved, the climate has changed; if they have not, last Tuesday was simply weather. This matters because it is the difference between an opinion based on one memory and a conclusion based on evidence.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. Climate is the average weather of a place, measured over a long period, usually thirty years or more.
- **Q3** (3 marks) The weather forecast tells him whether to harvest or spray tomorrow, but it says nothing about what to plant. What he needs is the average pattern: when the rains usually start, how long they last, how much rain falls, and how variable all of that is. That is climate, and it decides whether maize will mature before the rains stop, or whether he should choose a shorter-season or a drought-resistant variety instead. He also needs to know the range - how bad the worst year in twenty has been - because planting a crop that fails one year in five is a different decision from planting one that fails one year in twenty. A forecast for tomorrow cannot tell him any of it.

**19.2  19.2 Greenhouse Effects on the Environment**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Because climate varies naturally from year to year and from decade to decade, so any single measurement could be a fluctuation rather than a trend. If several independent lines of evidence all point the same way, the chance that they are all the same coincidence becomes very small. Independent means measured by different methods in different places: one thermometer record is not independent of another from the same station, but ice extent, sea level and the timing of the seasons are genuinely separate. Two kinds of evidence: temperature records, kept by weather stations all over the world for over a century, which show the average climbing; and the retreat of glaciers and the shrinking of Arctic sea ice, measured by satellite and by direct survey. Further kinds: sea level, measured by tide gauges and satellite, rising both because ice melts and because warm water expands; and the seasons shifting, with plants flowering earlier and rains arriving later.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. Temperature records from weather stations show the average rising. Glaciers are retreating and Arctic sea ice is shrinking. Sea level is rising. The seasons are shifting - rains arriving later, plants flowering earlier. Floods and droughts are both becoming more frequent.
- **Q6** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Ask the meteorological service or the agricultural extension office for the district's rainfall records over the last thirty years and look at the date the rains began in each year - the record settles it where memory does not. Ask older farmers in several different villages the same question: if they say the same thing independently and describe the same shift, that is worth far more than one person's recollection. Keep a record himself - write down the date the rains start every year from now on, so that in ten years there is data rather than memory. Watch for indirect signs, such as whether the planting calendar his father used still works.

**19.3  19.3 Sustainable Energy Choices and Scientific Ideas**

- **Q7** (4 marks) Sunlight is mostly short-wave radiation, and it passes through the atmosphere and warms the earth's surface. The warm surface radiates that energy back out, but as long-wave infrared radiation, which greenhouse gases - carbon dioxide, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide - absorb and re-radiate in all directions, including back downwards. So some of the heat that would have escaped into space is kept in. Without that effect at all, the earth would be roughly 30 C colder than it is and life as we know it would not exist: the natural greenhouse effect is what makes the planet habitable, and it is not a bad thing. What is a problem is the ENHANCED greenhouse effect. By burning coal, oil and gas, and by clearing and burning forest, we have added far more carbon dioxide to the air than was there before, so more of the outgoing heat is trapped and the average temperature climbs. The effect is not the problem; the extra gas is.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Burning coal, oil or gas for electricity, transport and industry: the carbon in the fuel combines with oxygen and goes straight into the air as carbon dioxide. Cutting down and burning forest: the carbon the trees had locked up in their wood is released at once when they burn, and gradually as the rest rots - and with the trees gone, far less carbon dioxide is taken out of the air in future. A third: making cement, which releases carbon dioxide from the limestone as well as from the fuel used to heat it.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Any three of: carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour, chlorofluorocarbons.

**19.4  19.4 Designing Local Energy Solutions**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Mitigation means acting on the cause - reducing the amount of greenhouse gas going into the air, so that the problem gets less worse in future. Adaptation means adjusting to the changes that are already happening, so that the damage is smaller. They are different timescales with different aims, and we need both. Mitigation the family could do: plant trees on their land and keep them, since a growing tree takes carbon dioxide out of the air; and stop burning crop residue, which releases it all at once. Adaptation: plant a shorter-season or drought-resistant variety of maize or millet, so the crop matures even if the rains start late or stop early - and this matters now, because the rains in the north are already less reliable. Another: dig a small dugout or set up a rainwater tank to carry water through a dry spell.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Because a changing climate makes the season less predictable, and different crops fail under different conditions: a late start suits one, a dry spell suits another, heavy rain a third. If all the land is in one crop, one bad season takes everything. With several crops, the failure of one is not the loss of the whole harvest, so the family still eats. Mixed cropping also keeps the ground covered, which cuts the loss of water from the soil and protects it from heavy rain; and if one of the crops is a legume it keeps the soil fertile without bought fertiliser. The whole point is spreading risk at a time when the risk can no longer be predicted.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. The rains arrive later and are less reliable, so crops fail more often. Floods and droughts are both more frequent, sometimes in the same year. Rising sea level is eroding the coast at Keta, Ada and along the western shore. Higher temperatures reduce the yields of cocoa and maize. The harmattan is shorter and the dry season hotter. Water supplies are less reliable.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) Sunlight passes easily through the clear plastic and warms the air and the surfaces inside the jar. The warm air then tries to radiate that heat back out, but the plastic will not let long-wave infrared through, so the heat is trapped and the temperature keeps climbing - 43 C in the covered jar against 34 C in the open one. This models the greenhouse effect: short-wave sunlight comes in, is absorbed, is re-radiated as long-wave heat, and something in between stops the heat getting out. In the atmosphere that something is the greenhouse gases rather than a sheet of plastic. The important difference is that a jar also traps heat by stopping CONVECTION - no warm air can rise out of it - whereas the real greenhouse effect works purely by absorbing and re-radiating radiation. The atmosphere is not a lid, it is a filter. So the model gets the radiation right and the containment wrong, and it is better to say so than to pretend the jar is the atmosphere.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Any three, each explained. Both jars the same size and shape, with the same volume of air, so that one is not simply heating a smaller amount of air. Both in the same place in the sun at the same time, so both receive the same sunlight. Both starting at the same temperature, so the comparison measures the heating rather than a difference that was there at the beginning. The same thermometer for both - or two thermometers checked against each other in the same water first, since otherwise the readings differ by however much the instruments disagree.
- **Q15** (3 marks) The plastic sheet that stopped heat getting in by radiation also stops it getting out the same way, so the covered jar loses heat more slowly as well as gaining it faster - the barrier works in both directions. That is actually a fair part of the model: greenhouse gases slow the escape of heat around the clock, not just during the day, which is why nights warm faster than days in a warming world. For an improvement: repeat the whole run on three separate days and take the mean, since one twenty-minute run under changing cloud is not much evidence. Or run a third jar, uncovered but with the same amount of air, as a second control. Or record the temperature every minute instead of every five, which shows the shape of the curve rather than five points.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the question that has to come first, because the confusion it addresses is universal and fatal to the rest of the strand. 'It rained heavily on Tuesday' is weather. Thirty years of records is climate. Pupils who cannot separate these will accept or dismiss climate change on the strength of one afternoon, and the point of 19.2 is that they should do neither.
- Q7 is the paper's best question and the one most likely to change a pupil's mind. The greenhouse effect is not a bad thing - without it the earth would be about 30 C colder and there would be nobody here to discuss it. The problem is the ENHANCED greenhouse effect. Getting pupils to make that distinction is worth more than any list of gases.
- Q13 asks pupils to say how the jar model is WRONG, not just how it is right. A jar traps heat partly by stopping convection; the atmosphere works purely by radiation. Pupils who can say what a model does not show have understood modelling, which is the skill the whole strand is quietly teaching.
- Q10 on mitigation versus adaptation is the one with consequences for Ghana. Mitigation is slow and global; adaptation is local and needed now. A northern farmer cannot wait for the world's emissions to fall - he needs a shorter-season variety this season. Both matter, and mixing them up wastes effort.
- The jar experiment needs two identical jars, two thermometers, and a sheet of clear plastic or cling film, run in direct sun for twenty minutes. It works best between 11am and 2pm. If the day is cloudy the difference will be smaller but still visible.
- A common error worth pre-empting: pupils put the thermometer in the sun rather than in the jar, or lift the plastic to read it, letting all the warm air out. Say both before they start.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**13.1  13.1 The Law of Conservation of Energy**

- **Q1** (4 marks) At the top of the slope the ball has gravitational POTENTIAL energy because of its height above the bottom. As it rolls down, that potential energy is converted into KINETIC energy and the ball speeds up. Once it is on the flat, friction with the ground and air resistance act against its motion, so the kinetic energy is gradually converted into HEAT - warming the ball, the ground and the air very slightly - and into SOUND. So the ball slows and stops. The energy has not been destroyed: there is exactly as much as there was at the top. But it is now spread out as low-grade heat in the surroundings, far too scattered to be gathered back together and used again. Conservation of energy is not the same as conservation of usefulness.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: gravitational potential, kinetic, heat, light, sound, chemical, electrical, nuclear, elastic (strain).
- **Q3** (3 marks) (a) Chemical energy stored in the cells becomes electrical energy in the circuit, which becomes light and heat at the bulb. (b) Chemical energy stored in the charcoal becomes heat and light. (c) Pulling back: kinetic energy from your arm becomes elastic potential energy stored in the bent bow and stretched string. On release: that elastic potential energy becomes kinetic energy of the string and the arrow, with some heat and sound.

**13.2  13.2 Energy Conversion**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Water held behind the dam: gravitational POTENTIAL energy, because it is high up. Water falling down the pipe: KINETIC energy, as the potential energy is converted into movement. Water striking the turbine: KINETIC energy of the spinning turbine and shaft. Generator: the spinning shaft drives the generator and the output is ELECTRICAL energy, carried by cables to homes, where it becomes light, heat or kinetic energy depending on the appliance. At every stage some energy leaves the useful path as heat - friction between the water and the pipe, friction in the turbine bearings, electrical resistance in the generator windings - and as sound.
- **Q5** (3 marks) At every conversion a little energy leaves the useful path. Some water splashes or leaks past the turbine without driving it. Friction between the water and the pipe wall, and in the turbine bearings, turns energy into heat. The generator has resistance in its windings, which warms it, and friction in its own bearings. Turbulence and the impact of the water make sound. All of that is energy that still exists but is no longer in the electrical output. So the electrical energy out is less than the potential energy in, and the difference has become heat in the water, the machine and the air, plus a little sound. Nothing has been destroyed - the useful output is simply smaller than the input.
- **Q6** (3 marks) The fraction of the energy put in that comes out in the useful form, usually given as a percentage: efficiency = (useful energy output / total energy input) x 100%. The rest is not destroyed, but has been converted into forms that are not wanted.

**13.3  13.3 Everyday Examples of Energy Conversion**

- **Q7** (4 marks) The law states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, and the total amount in a closed system stays constant. The pupil is right that none of the fuel's energy is destroyed, but wrong to think that means it stays available. As the car runs, the chemical energy in the fuel is converted into kinetic energy, heat and sound. The heat goes into the engine, the exhaust gases, the tyres, the road and the air, where it spreads out. Once energy is spread out as low-grade heat it cannot be gathered back up and concentrated again to drive the car. So the car does not run for ever - not because the energy has gone, but because it has become unavailable. This is the difference between conserving energy and conserving its usefulness.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Total energy out = 60 J + 30 J + 10 J = 100 J, which is exactly the energy put in. Every joule is accounted for, so the law holds. Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input x 100% = 60 / 100 x 100 = 60%.
- **Q9** (3 marks) A Sankey diagram is an energy-flow diagram drawn to scale. The width of each band is proportional to the amount of energy flowing along that path. One band carries the total input in, and it splits into a band for the useful output and separate bands for each loss, so you can see at a glance how much is wasted and where it goes.

**13.4  13.4 Conserving Energy for Future Use**

- **Q10** (4 marks) A renewable source is one that natural processes replace at least as fast as we use it, so the stock does not run down - sun, wind, flowing water, geothermal heat, and biomass that is properly managed. A non-renewable source is a fixed stock laid down over millions of years that we are using far faster than it can ever be replaced - oil, natural gas, coal, uranium, peat; once it is burnt it is gone for good. Firewood is renewable only if trees are replanted and allowed to grow at least as fast as they are cut. In parts of Ghana wood is taken for firewood and charcoal faster than it regrows, and there it behaves exactly like a non-renewable source: the stock falls year by year. Being renewable is not a property of the material alone, it is a property of how fast we use it.
- **Q11** (3 marks) For cooking: biogas made from animal dung and crop waste in a digester - the village has animals, the gas burns cleanly, and the slurry left over is a rich fertiliser for the fields. A well-managed woodlot is an acceptable alternative, but only if the village plants as fast as it cuts. For lighting: solar, because the north has long hours of strong sunshine for much of the year with little cloud. A panel and a battery need no fuel and no connection to the national grid, which matters in a remote village, and the running cost is almost nothing.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Any three, each with a use. Crude oil - petrol and diesel for vehicles. Natural gas - cooking and power stations. Coal - power stations and industry. Uranium - nuclear power stations. Peat - cut, dried and burnt as a domestic fuel.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) Held at the drop height, the ball has gravitational POTENTIAL energy. As it falls that becomes KINETIC energy, and it is moving fastest just before it strikes the floor. On impact the ball squashes, so the kinetic energy becomes ELASTIC potential energy in the deformed rubber and the compressed air inside; as it springs back, that elastic energy becomes kinetic energy again and the ball leaves the floor. But not all of it comes back. Some was turned into heat by internal friction as the rubber deformed, some into sound, and some into heating the floor. So the ball leaves the floor with less kinetic energy than it arrived with, rises to a lower height, and each bounce is about 62% of the one before. Energy is conserved - the total is unchanged - but with every bounce more of it is spread out as heat and sound, and less is left in the ball as movement.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Dropped from 100 cm the first bounce is 62 cm, so about 62% - a fraction of 0.62 - of the drop height. The second bounce is 38 cm, and 38 / 62 = 0.61, again about 62% of the first bounce. So each bounce reaches roughly 0.62 of the height before it. Dropped from 40 cm: the first bounce is about 0.62 x 40 = 25 cm, and the second is about 0.62 x 25 = 15.5 cm, so roughly 15 or 16 cm. Accept any answer in the range 15-16 cm, and accept a slightly different constant such as 0.6 if the pupil has used it consistently.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each with a fix. The top of the bounce lasts only an instant, so it is hard to read against the ruler - have one pupil watch from directly in front at eye level and call it out, or film the bounce and step through it frame by frame. Parallax: the eye must be level with the top of the ball; if it is above or below, the reading is wrong - so the observer should kneel or stand to get level. The ball may not bounce straight up or may spin - use a flat hard floor and release it cleanly without pushing. Always read the same part of the ball each time, so the measurement is consistent.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q7 is the question the whole strand exists to answer, and it is the one that catches the able pupils as well as the weak ones. 'Energy cannot be destroyed, so why does the car stop?' The answer is the distinction between conservation and AVAILABILITY: the energy is all still there, spread out as low-grade heat. Pupils who reach for 'it is used up' have missed the law they have just stated. Worth doing at the board before the class meets the practical.
- Q1 is the same idea in a simpler setting, and it is a good one to set first. The sentence to aim for is 'it has not gone, it has spread out'.
- Q10 on firewood is where 13.4 stops being a list. Being renewable is not a property of the material - it is a property of the rate at which we take it. In much of Ghana firewood is being cut faster than it regrows, so in practice it is behaving as a non-renewable source. Pupils in the north will have seen this.
- Q5 and Q8 are the pair that turn the law into arithmetic. Q8 is deliberately easy - 60 + 30 + 10 = 100 - so the pupil who gets it wrong has an accounting problem, not a physics problem.
- The bouncing-ball practical needs a metre rule clamped vertically, a hard floor (a concrete or tiled one, not a mat), and a ball with a good bounce - a tennis ball or a rubber ball, not a football. The awkward part is reading the top of the bounce; a phone video stepped through frame by frame is worth the trouble if you have one.
- Watch for pupils who throw the ball down instead of releasing it - that adds energy at the start and the first bounce comes out anomalously high. The instruction to release, not throw, is worth saying twice.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**5.1  5.1 What are Plant Nutrients?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Nitrogen. The diagram links nitrogen with the leaves and shoots, and pale yellow leaves are its deficiency symptom. The reason the oldest leaves show it first is that nitrogen can be moved about inside the plant. When the soil cannot supply enough, the plant takes the nitrogen out of its oldest, lowest leaves and moves it up to the young growing leaves at the top, because new growth matters more to the plant than old leaves do. So the old leaves are drained first and go yellow, while the young ones stay green for a while longer. As the shortage gets worse the yellowing spreads upwards.
- **Q2** (2 marks) Any two, each with a correct job. Nitrogen - builds the leaves and shoots, so the plant grows green and tall. Phosphorus - builds the roots, flowers and seeds. Potassium - strengthens the stem and helps the fruit and seeds fill.

**5.2  5.2 Organic and Inorganic Nutrient Sources**

- **Q3** (3 marks) Inorganic. The diagram sorts nutrient sources by where they come from, not by whether they contain carbon: organic means it comes from once-living plants or animals, and inorganic means it is mined from rock or made in a factory. Urea is made in a factory, so it goes on the inorganic side even though it is a nitrogen fertiliser like compost or manure. The test is the SOURCE, not the nutrient it supplies.
- **Q4** (3 marks) It is an ORGANIC nutrient source - the diagram lists crop residue, and the stalks and leaves are dead plant material, so they come from once-living things. It will not feed the next crop straight away because the nutrients in it are still locked up inside the dead tissue. They are only released as micro-organisms in the soil rot the material down, and that takes time - weeks or months. Until it has decayed, the nutrients are there but the plant roots cannot take them up. That is exactly why organic sources are described as slow.

**5.3  5.3 Differences Between Organic and Inorganic Fertilizers**

- **Q5** (4 marks) Because they do different jobs, and the crop needs both done in the same season. Inorganic fertiliser releases its nutrients at once, so it can feed a hungry crop at the moment the crop needs it - a young maize plant at three weeks cannot wait months for compost to rot. It is also concentrated, so a small bag carries a lot of nutrient, which is what makes it possible to apply enough. Organic material, meanwhile, is slow and bulky: it builds the soil for next season and the seasons after, but it cannot meet a sudden demand. So the farmer uses the inorganic fertiliser to feed THIS crop and the organic matter to build the soil for the ones that follow.
- **Q6** (3 marks) The field given NPK loses more. The diagram gives the reason: NPK has a high risk of leaching, while compost has little. Inorganic fertiliser dissolves as soon as it is wet, so the nutrients are sitting in the soil water in a form that rain can simply carry down past the roots and away. Compost holds its nutrients inside solid decaying material that has to be rotted down first, so there is far less dissolved nutrient in the water for the rain to wash out. The NPK is not only wasted, it can pollute the watercourse it drains into.

**5.4  5.4 Physical Characteristics of Plant Nutrients**

- **Q7** (4 marks) Look at the colour, the shape of the pieces and whether anything is recognisable. Compost is dark brown to black and made of crumbs and flakes of all different shapes and sizes, it smells of damp earth, and you can often still pick out a bit of leaf or stem. NPK granules are pale - grey, white or pinkish - every granule is the same size and round, there is little smell, and nothing in it is recognisable. They look different because they are made differently. Compost is decayed plant and animal matter, so it is a jumble of whatever went into the heap, broken down unevenly. NPK is manufactured: the nutrients are mixed to a set recipe and then formed into uniform granules, so every one matches the next.
- **Q8** (3 marks) What matters is what the fertiliser does, not where it came from. The diagram compares the two on things that affect the crop: how fast the nutrients are released, how much nutrient there is per kilogram, what it does to the soil, how long it lasts, and how easily it is washed away. On some of those compost is better, and on others NPK is better - NPK carries far more nutrient per kilogram and feeds the crop immediately. Calling one 'natural' tells you none of that. A farmer choosing between them needs to know whether the crop needs feeding now or whether the soil needs building, and that is a question about the crop, not about whether the bag came from a heap or a factory.

**5.5  5.5 How Plant Nutrients Are Applied in the Field**

- **Q9** (4 marks) Side-dressing. The diagram shows the fertiliser being placed in a band beside the row while the crop is growing, which is exactly this situation - the crop is already up and needs feeding now. It is better than broadcasting because the band is put right next to the roots, so the nutrient is where the plant can reach it and little is wasted. Broadcasting scatters the fertiliser over the whole field, so most of it lands between the rows where there are no roots to take it up; that part is wasted, and on a sloping field it washes away. Broadcasting is also for before planting, and this crop is already growing.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Fertiliser is a salt, and against the stem it draws water out of the living tissue by osmosis and burns it. A ring of concentrated fertiliser touching the stem scorches the bark and can kill the growing point, which kills the whole plant. The ring is placed out at the edge of the root spread for two reasons: that is where the feeding roots actually are, and it keeps the fertiliser clear of the stem so the stem is not damaged.

**5.6  5.6 Practical Application in the School Garden**

- **Q11** (4 marks) The paths let pupils reach every bed to weed, water, apply fertiliser and harvest without having to tread on the soil the crops are growing in. Walking on the beds would compact the soil, pressing the particles together and squeezing out the air spaces between them. Once that happens the roots cannot get the oxygen they need for respiration, water drains poorly and runs off the surface instead of soaking in, and the roots cannot push through the hard ground. Compacted soil also makes it much harder for the crop to take up nutrients even when they are present. The paths confine the trampling to ground where nothing is expected to grow.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. NPK costs money and compost often does not, so using compost on some beds keeps the cost down while still feeding the crop. Rotating the compost around the beds over the years builds up the soil everywhere in the end, rather than leaving the NPK beds dependent on bought fertiliser for ever. Different crops have different demands - a hungry crop like maize is worth the expense of NPK, while another may do well enough on compost. And it lets the school compare the two side by side on its own ground, which is worth more to the pupils than being told.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) NPK 15-15-15, in Plot C, produced the tallest maize at 86 cm. The maize with nothing added, in Plot A, reached 42 cm. The difference is 86 - 42 = 44 cm, so the NPK maize was 44 cm taller. For comparison, the compost plot reached 68 cm, which is 26 cm taller than the control, so compost also had a clear effect but a smaller one than NPK over these six weeks.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Plot A is the control, and without it the experiment shows nothing. It measures what the maize does on its own in that soil, with that water and that weather. Because every other condition is the same across the plots, any difference between A and the others must be down to the fertiliser. If Plot A were missing, a height of 86 cm in Plot C would be meaningless - the maize might have grown that tall anyway on this soil, and you would have no way of telling whether the NPK made any difference at all or whether the good soil and the rain did it all.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. The same variety of maize in every plot, because a taller variety would grow taller whatever it was fed, and the comparison would be worthless. The same soil in every plot, because a richer soil would feed the plants itself and you could not tell whether the fertiliser or the soil produced the extra growth. The same watering, because a plot that got more water would grow better regardless of the fertiliser. The same spacing, because crowded plants compete with each other for light, water and nutrients and are stunted for that reason. The same plot size, so that the mean height is worked out from a fair number of plants in each case.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 78% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 42% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the best question in the paper and the one most pupils will get wrong. They will name nitrogen happily - the diagram gives them the symptom - and then say the oldest leaves yellow 'because they are oldest'. The real answer is that nitrogen is MOBILE inside the plant: the plant strips it out of the old leaves and sends it to the growing tip, so the old leaves pay first. Teach it as 'the plant sacrifices the old to feed the new'.
- Q3 on urea is the classification trap. Pupils reason 'urea contains carbon, so it is organic'. The diagram sorts by SOURCE, not by chemistry: once-living versus mined or manufactured. Urea is made in a factory, so it is inorganic. Expect the argument and settle it early.
- Q6 on leaching after heavy rain is worth doing as a class discussion, because it is the reason inorganic fertiliser is both expensive and environmentally costly, and it makes the case for organic matter concrete rather than pious.
- Q10 on why ring application must not touch the stem is the one where pupils have real experience to draw on - many have seen a plant 'burnt' by fertiliser. Let them say what they saw, then give them the reason: the salt draws water out of the living tissue by osmosis.
- The maize experiment in Fig. 7 is cheap to run in a school garden with three small plots and a metre rule, and the numbers in the table are realistic for six weeks. Run it for real if the timing allows; measuring their own plants once a week makes Q13 to Q15 easy and makes the idea of a control obvious.
- If you want a calculation extension, ask pupils to work out how many maize plants fit Bed 1 at 75 cm by 90 cm spacing. I left this out of the paper because the bed dimensions on the plan are schematic rather than to scale, and the sum would be arguable - but with real bed measurements from your own garden it works well.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**7.1  7.1 What is Food? Nutrients and Their Importance**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Maize supplies carbohydrate and fish supplies protein, so two of the six classes are covered and that is enough to fill the stomach and stop hunger. But the diagram shows six classes, and the other four are missing: fats and oil, vitamins, minerals and water. Not feeling hungry is not the test - a balanced diet means having all the classes in the right amounts, and each missing one has its own consequence. Without vitamin C the gums bleed and wounds heal slowly; without iron the blood cannot carry oxygen properly and the person is anaemic and tired; without calcium the bones stay weak; without enough fat the body cannot absorb some vitamins at all. So the person is fed but not nourished.
- **Q2** (2 marks) Any two, each with a correct source: carbohydrate - bread, rice, yam, maize; protein - fish, eggs, beans, meat; fats and oil - palm oil, butter, nuts; vitamins - fruit and vegetables; minerals - milk, salt, green leaves; water - clean drinking water.

**7.2  7.2 Why Humans Need to Eat**

- **Q3** (3 marks) The diagram shows that body mass depends on the BALANCE between energy in and energy out, not on eating fat as such. Cutting out fat does reduce the energy coming in, so on that point the pupil is right. But it is only half the answer, because the other side of the balance matters just as much: a person who eats only a little fat but takes in more carbohydrate than they use will still store the excess as body fat and gain weight. The body converts surplus energy from any class of food into stored fat. To lose weight the person must either take in less energy or use more, so that energy out exceeds energy in.

**7.3  7.3 The Digestive System: Parts of the Alimentary Canal**

- **Q4** (4 marks) The canal has to be long because its two jobs - digesting the food and absorbing the digested products - both need time and surface. A long tube gives the food time to pass slowly enough for the enzymes to finish their work, and it gives a large enough area of wall for the products to be absorbed through. If a large part of the small intestine were removed, both would suffer: the food would pass through too quickly for digestion to be completed, and there would be far less wall to absorb through. The undigested, unabsorbed food would be passed out as diarrhoea, and the person would lose weight and become malnourished even while eating normally.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Being part of the alimentary canal is about being part of the ROUTE the food takes, not about carrying out digestion. The canal is defined as the tube running from the mouth to the anus, and the oesophagus is a section of that tube. But the different sections have different jobs, and the oesophagus's job is only to carry the food - its muscles squeeze the food downwards in waves to the stomach. The diagram makes the point by listing 'nothing' in the chemical column for the oesophagus: it is a passage, not a place where food is broken down.

**7.4  7.4 What Happens to Food at Each Stage of Digestion**

- **Q6** (3 marks) Mechanical digestion breaks the food into smaller pieces without changing what it is - the teeth chew and grind it in the mouth, or the stomach wall churns it into a liquid, and it is still the same substance, only in smaller bits. Chemical digestion changes the food into a DIFFERENT substance, using enzymes and acid - for example saliva beginning to turn starch into sugar, or the stomach's enzymes attacking protein. One changes the size, the other changes the substance.
- **Q7** (4 marks) Chewing is mechanical digestion, and its effect is to break the food into many small pieces. Doing that greatly increases the SURFACE AREA of the food, and the enzymes that do the chemical digestion later can only attack the surface they can reach. So the more the food is broken up, the more of it the enzymes in the stomach and small intestine can work on at the same time, and the faster and more completely the chemical digestion goes. Chewing also mixes the food thoroughly with saliva and makes it easier to swallow. So although chewing does not itself finish any chemical digestion, it prepares the food so that the chemical digestion which follows can do its job properly.

**7.5  7.5 End Products of Digestion: Starch, Protein and Fats**

- **Q8** (3 marks) The diagram shows that glucose is the END PRODUCT of starch digestion - it is already small and soluble, so it is in exactly the form the body can use. Because it needs no further digesting, it can be put directly into the blood and the whole digestive system is bypassed. The patient is getting the product their gut would have produced but cannot, delivered by a route that does not depend on the gut working.
- **Q9** (4 marks) Although starch is built from glucose units, it is one enormous molecule, and it is far too big to pass through the wall of the small intestine and into the blood. It is also insoluble. The glucose units have to be separated from one another first, because only the individual small, soluble glucose molecules are able to cross the gut wall. So the body is not rejecting the glucose - it simply cannot reach it while it is locked up in the large molecule. Digestion is the unlocking, and until it happens the glucose in the starch is unavailable.

**7.6  7.6 Absorption of Digested Food in the Small Intestine**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Any two, each explained. There are thousands of villi, and the folds they make give an enormously large surface area, so a great deal of digested food can pass through the wall at the same moment. The wall of each villus is only one cell thick, so the food has a very short distance to travel to get into the blood, which makes diffusion quick. Each villus has a rich blood supply, and the blood carries the absorbed food away immediately, which keeps the concentration difference steep so that more food keeps diffusing in. A villus also has a lacteal, so fats are carried away too.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Fats pass into the LACTEAL, not into the blood capillary. The diagram shows the two vessels separately, with glucose and amino acids going to the capillary and fats to the lacteal. They take a different route because the products of fat digestion are handled differently by the body - they are taken up into the lymphatic system rather than being carried straight to the liver in the blood.

**7.7  7.7 Food Tests: Starch, Glucose, Protein, Fats and Oils**

- **Q12** (3 marks) Add a few drops of iodine solution to the food sample - or to a solution or paste made from it - in a test tube or on a white tile. Iodine starts brown. If starch is present the colour changes to blue-black; if starch is absent it stays brown. A control using pure water or a sample known to contain no starch is run alongside for comparison.
- **Q13** (3 marks) A green colour still shows that a reducing sugar such as glucose is present - the test has not failed, and the answer is not 'no sugar'. Benedict's is not simply a yes-or-no test: the colour it turns depends on roughly HOW MUCH reducing sugar there is. Brick-red means a lot; orange or green means a smaller amount. So the pupil's sample contains some glucose, but less of it than a sample giving brick-red. The pupil should report it as a positive result for a small amount of reducing sugar, and could compare the colour against known samples to estimate how much.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q14** (4 marks) Samples B and D contain starch - the iodine in those two tubes changed from brown to blue-black, which is the positive result, while A and C stayed brown. To check the result is reliable I would repeat the test: carry it out again on fresh portions of each of the four samples, and check that the same two give blue-black a second time. I would also make the comparison fair by using the same number of drops of iodine in every tube and the same amount of each sample. Results that can be repeated are the ones worth trusting.
- **Q15** (3 marks) The iodine test tests for STARCH and for nothing else. All the results show is that A and C contain no detectable starch - they say nothing at all about glucose, protein, fats, vitamins or minerals. Sample A or C could be almost pure protein and the iodine test would still stay brown, because iodine does not react with protein. To claim a sample contains no nutrients you would have to test it separately for each class, using Benedict's for glucose, Biuret for protein and ethanol for fats. A negative result in one test is only ever evidence about that one nutrient.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 78% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q9 is the question that separates pupils who have the idea from those who have the words. 'Starch is made of glucose, so why can't the body use it?' The answer is size and solubility: the glucose is there, but locked inside a molecule too big to cross the gut wall. Pupils who say 'it is too big' without saying WHY that matters - it cannot get through into the blood - have not finished.
- Q7 on chewing is a surface-area question dressed up as a health-advice question. The chain is: chew, smaller pieces, larger surface area, more enzymes working at once, faster complete digestion. Four links, four marks. Most pupils stop at 'it helps you swallow'.
- Q3 on cutting out fat is the misconception I most want caught. Body mass is a BALANCE, and surplus carbohydrate is stored as fat just as surely as eaten fat is. Pupils who get this have understood 7.2 rather than memorised it.
- Q13 on the green Benedict's result is worth doing even if you have covered food tests before, because pupils treat these tests as pass or fail. They are not - the colour indicates roughly how much. A green result is a POSITIVE result for a small amount.
- Q15 is the same lesson at the level of experimental reasoning: a negative result in one test is evidence about one nutrient only. Pupils write 'contains no nutrients' straight after an iodine test. Insist they name the nutrient the test actually looked for.
- Fig. 8 is a real experiment that any school can run with iodine and four samples - floor, gari, sugar solution and cooked rice work well and give two positives and two negatives. Get pupils to predict first, then test; the predictions are where the thinking shows.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**3.1  3.1 Natural Sources of Water**

- **Q1** (4 marks) The water table is the level below which the pores and cracks in the soil and rock are full of water; above it the ground is only damp and holds no free water that can be drawn off. So a well or a borehole must be dug down past that level so that water can seep in through the sides and collect at the bottom. During a long drought, little or no rain soaks into the ground to replace what is drawn out, so the water table falls. If it falls below the bottom of the well, the well yields nothing - it has run dry. A borehole is drilled much deeper precisely so that it still reaches water when the table drops, which is why boreholes keep supplying water after shallow wells have failed.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three, each correctly classified. Stream - surface. River - surface. Pond - surface. Spring - underground water coming to the surface. Well - underground. Borehole - underground.
- **Q3** (2 marks) Any two of: rain, stream, river, pond, spring, well, borehole.

**3.2  3.2 Stages of the Water Cycle: Evaporation, Condensation, Precipitation and Transpiration**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Evaporation needs energy. To turn liquid water into vapour, the molecules have to be given enough energy to break free of the liquid, and on this planet the sun supplies that energy. Without it, evaporation from the sea would almost stop. No vapour would rise, so no clouds would form, and rain would cease. The water already on the land would drain into the sea, rivers would run down and then dry, and the water table would not be recharged. The sun is the pump that drives the whole cycle; everything else in it is consequence.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Transpiration. A forest carries an enormous total area of leaf surface, and every leaf is giving off water vapour, so the amount added up over the whole canopy is very large - often larger than the water evaporating from the soil beneath. The canopy also shades the ground, which keeps the soil cooler and so reduces direct evaporation from it. Together those two effects mean that in a forest the plants, not the soil, are the main source of water vapour in the air.

**3.3  3.3 Why the Water Cycle is a Repeated Pattern in Nature**

- **Q6** (4 marks) A closed system is one in which nothing enters or leaves overall: the total amount stays the same and everything that happens is a change of form or a change of place. Very little water escapes into space and very little arrives from it, so the earth's stock of water is essentially fixed. What the cycle does is move it about and change it - liquid to vapour to liquid, sea to air to land and back again. Because no water is used up, the water in a raindrop today is made of molecules that have already been through countless previous cycles: through oceans, clouds, glaciers, rivers and living things. The cycle is a repeated pattern because the same water is used over and over rather than replaced.
- **Q7** (3 marks) The arrows join up: stage 6 collects the water and returns it to where stage 1 begins, so the loop closes on itself. That means any stage could be called the first - you can start at condensation, or at rain, or at collection, and you will still go through all the others and arrive back where you started. The numbers are only a convenient way of listing the stages so they can be talked about; they are not an order in time. A cycle by definition has no beginning and no end.

**3.4  3.4 Importance of the Water Cycle to the Environment**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Distillation means separating a liquid from the solids dissolved in it by turning the liquid into vapour and then back into liquid again. When sea water evaporates, only the water molecules leave: the salt and everything else dissolved in the sea has far too high a boiling point to evaporate at ordinary temperatures, so it is left behind in the sea. The vapour that rises is therefore pure water, and when it condenses the droplets are fresh. That is why rain is fresh despite coming mostly from the sea, and why the cycle is the earth's fresh-water supply: it is a natural distillation plant that takes salty water and delivers fresh water onto the land, over and over, with no machinery and no fuel other than the sun.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. It supplies fresh water to rivers, lakes, streams and the water table, which plants, animals and people depend on. It carries water from the sea inland, so that places far from the coast still get rain. It recharges wells and boreholes. It returns water to the air and so cools and moistens it. It makes plant growth possible, and therefore food.

**3.5  3.5 The Water Cycle and Weather Patterns**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Most of the water vapour in the air evaporates from the sea, because that is where most of the earth's water is and where it is most exposed. The air moving inland carries that moisture with it, and as it rises and cools the vapour condenses into cloud and then falls as rain. The heaviest rain therefore falls soon after the air leaves the sea - that is, near the coast. By the time the same air has travelled far inland it has already shed much of its moisture, so there is less left to fall. That is why rainfall decreases with distance from the sea, which the diagram shows by the clouds getting smaller and the rain thinner as they move inland.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Trees return a great deal of water to the air by transpiration, and in forest that source is often larger than evaporation from the ground. Remove the trees and that water no longer enters the air, so there is less moisture available to condense into cloud and fall as rain. The forest also shades and cools the ground and slows the run-off that would otherwise rush straight to the sea. So the air passing over the cleared land picks up less moisture than it used to, and places downwind of it receive less rain.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q12** (4 marks) Fastest to slowest: D (18 ml left), A (35 ml), C (62 ml), B (78 ml). Comparing A with B shows that warmth speeds evaporation - same wide dish, but the one in the sun lost far more than the one in the shade. Comparing A with C shows that a larger surface area speeds it - same sun, but the wide dish lost more than the narrow one, because there is more surface for molecules to escape from. Comparing D with A shows that moving air speeds it - same dish and same sun, but the dish with a fan blowing over it lost most of all.
- **Q13** (3 marks) In both dishes the molecules are moving at a range of speeds, and the fastest ones near the surface escape into the air as vapour. In dish A that vapour collects in the still air just above the water, so the air there becomes humid and some of the escaped molecules fall back into the liquid. In dish D the fan continually sweeps the vapour away and replaces it with drier air, so the air above the water never becomes humid and molecules that escape are not coming back. Net escape stays fast, so the water level drops quicker.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Every dish must start with the same volume of water - 100 ml - because if one started with less there would be less to lose and you could not compare what is left. All four must be left for the same three days, because a dish left longer would lose more whatever its conditions. Where a pair is being compared, the two dishes must be the same size and shape so that surface area is not a second difference. The water in every dish should start at the same temperature.
- **Q15** (3 marks) He should set up two identical dishes with the same volume of water, in the same place, for the same length of time, and put a lid on one while leaving the other open - so the lid is the only difference. Then he measures how much water is left in each. He should expect the covered dish to lose far less. The lid traps the vapour, so the air in the space above the water quickly becomes saturated: as many molecules fall back in as escape, and net evaporation almost stops. Water that condenses on the underside of the lid also drips back into the dish.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 78% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q8 is the best question in the paper. Every pupil knows rain is fresh and the sea is salt, and almost none can say why. The answer is distillation: only water molecules evaporate, the salt stays behind. If they can explain that, they understand the cycle as a process rather than a picture to copy.
- Q6 on the closed system is where the 'repeated pattern' wording of 3.3 becomes real. Pupils will say 'the water goes round and round' without grasping that it is the SAME water. Push them on it: no water is made and none is destroyed, so today's rain has been through the cycle before, many times.
- Q7 on the numbering is a small question that catches a real confusion. Pupils treat the numbering as a sequence in time and look for a first stage. The arrows close the loop, so there isn't one.
- Q11 on deforestation reducing downwind rainfall is deliberately cross-topic - it links 3.5 to the forest's role and rewards pupils who see transpiration as a real contribution rather than a label on a diagram.
- The evaporation experiment in Fig. 6 needs four shallow dishes, a measuring cylinder, and a fan if you have one. Three days is enough to give the differences in the table. The particle explanation in Q13 is the one pupils find hardest: the fan does not change the water, it removes the vapour that has already left so fewer molecules return.
- If you have no fan, prop a book to make a draught or simply place one dish in a breeze; the direction of the result is the same and the numbers are still usable.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**9.1  9.1 What is an Ecosystem?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) A habitat is only the place where an organism lives. An ecosystem is the community of living things together with the non-living parts, all interacting as one system. The diagram shows both: the fish, frog, dragonfly, plants and reeds are the living part, and the water, the sunlight, the stones and the temperature are the non-living part. What makes it an ecosystem is that they INTERACT - the plants use the sunlight to make food, the fish and insects feed on the plants, the frog feeds on the insects, and wastes and dead remains are broken back down in the water.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any two with a reason: SUNLIGHT - the plants need it to make their food by photosynthesis, so without it no food enters the ecosystem at all. WATER - it is the habitat itself; the fish breathe the oxygen dissolved in it, the plants root in it, and every organism needs it to stay alive. STONES - they give surfaces for plants to root on and places for small animals to hide from predators. TEMPERATURE - it controls how fast the organisms grow and how much oxygen the water can hold.

**9.2  9.2 Types of Ecosystems: Terrestrial, Aquatic and Arboreal**

- **Q3** (4 marks) Any two, organism plus adaptation: AQUATIC - fish have gills to take oxygen out of the water and a streamlined body and fins to swim. TERRESTRIAL - grazing animals have long legs and hooves for running across open ground away from predators, and flat teeth for cropping grass. ARBOREAL - monkeys and lizards have gripping hands, feet or claws for holding branches, and birds have wings and light bones for moving between trees.
- **Q4** (3 marks) A frog breathes partly through its skin, which must stay moist for oxygen to dissolve into it, and it must return to water to lay its eggs because they have no shell. In a dry terrestrial habitat it would lose water through its skin faster than it could replace it and would dry out, and any eggs it laid would dry up too.

**9.3  9.3 Components of an Ecosystem: Biotic and Abiotic Factors**

- **Q5** (3 marks) LIVING (biotic): 3 water lily, 5 fish, 6 dragonfly, 8 frog. NON-LIVING (abiotic): 1 sunlight, 2 water, 4 stones, 7 temperature.
- **Q6** (3 marks) SUNLIGHT - the water lilies and reeds could not photosynthesise, so they would stop making food and would die. Every animal that feeds on them, and every animal that feeds on those, would then run out of food, so the whole pond would collapse. OR WATER - there would be no habitat at all and every organism in it would die. OR OXYGEN IN THE WATER - the fish would suffocate.
- **Q7** (4 marks) An ecosystem is defined by the things in it and how they INTERACT, not by where those things come from. Sunlight reaches the water and the plants in the pond use it to make their food; without it, no energy would enter the system at all. Because the living parts depend on it, it is one of the abiotic components of the ecosystem, even though it arrives from outside. Rain falling in, and leaves blowing in, are part of the pond ecosystem for exactly the same reason.

**9.4  9.4 How Components of an Ecosystem Interact**

- **Q8** (3 marks) The arrow means IS EATEN BY, and it shows the direction in which the energy and the food pass. The direction matters because energy only flows one way - from the organism being eaten to the organism that eats it. An arrow drawn the wrong way round would say that the hawk is eaten by the lizard, which is the wrong way round and changes the meaning of the whole chain.
- **Q9** (4 marks) The grasshoppers would increase at first, because the animals that were eating them are gone. As the grasshopper population grows, the grasshoppers eat more and more of the plants, so the number of plants falls. Eventually the plants cannot support the large grasshopper population, the grasshoppers run short of food and starve, and their numbers crash back down. So the number rises sharply and then falls again.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals and animal waste, and in doing so they return the nutrients locked up in them back to the soil and the water. Without them, dead remains would pile up and the nutrients in them would stay locked away. The plants would run short of the nutrients they need to grow, so less food would be made, and the whole ecosystem would slowly run down.

**9.5  9.5 Interdependence of Organisms in an Ecosystem**

- **Q11** (3 marks) Any two with four or more links and arrows pointing the right way, e.g. grass --> grasshopper --> toad --> hawk;  maize --> caterpillar --> bird --> snake;  leaves --> mouse --> bird --> hawk;  grass --> mouse --> snake. (The arrow means 'is eaten by'.)
- **Q12** (4 marks) In a single chain each animal has only one source of food, so if that one link fails everything above it loses its only supply and the chain collapses. In a web an animal has alternatives: if the grasshoppers die out, the toad can still eat caterpillars. Because the failure of one link can be absorbed by switching to another, the web as a whole survives a change that would destroy a chain.
- **Q13** (3 marks) Any two effects, with the reasoning: the animals that feed on grasshoppers - the lizard, the toad and the bird - would have less food, so their numbers would fall unless they can switch to caterpillars or mice. The plants the grasshoppers ate - grass and maize - would be eaten less, so they would grow more thickly. The hawk and the snake would eventually be affected too, because the animals they eat have become fewer.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q14** (4 marks) Throw the quadrat at random, count every plant of the kind you are studying that lies INSIDE the square, and record the number. Do the same in several different places, add the counts together and divide by the number of throws to get an average number per square metre. Then multiply that average by the total area of the field. You throw it more than once because one square may land on a patch that is unusually bare or unusually thick - several throws and an average give a fairer estimate of the whole field.
- **Q15** (2 marks) Counting the whole field would take far too long and it is very easy to miss plants or to count the same one twice, so the answer would probably be wrong anyway. Sampling a few squares is quick and, if the samples are fair, gives an answer that is close enough for the purpose.
