## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 72% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q8 is the one to insist on, and it is where marks are lost for a reason nothing to do with biology. Pupils know the feeding order perfectly well and then draw every arrow backwards. 'The arrow means IS EATEN BY' should be said in every lesson until it is automatic. Give 0 for a chain with the arrows reversed - the direction IS the answer.
- Q9 is the population question and pupils almost always stop half way. They say 'the grasshoppers increase' and stop. The full answer has three steps: increase, then the plants get eaten down, then the grasshoppers starve and crash. Mark it as three points, not one, and teach the shape.
- Q7 is the most abstract and the best test of whether a pupil has understood what an ecosystem IS. The objection - 'sunlight comes from outside so it cannot be part of the pond' - is a good objection, and the answer is that membership comes from interaction, not from location. Expect very few pupils to get this without being taught it.
- Q12, on why a web is more stable than a chain, is the hardest 'why' in the paper. The word to aim for is ALTERNATIVES: an animal with two food sources survives the loss of one. Pupils who answer 'because there are more animals' have not reached it.
- The quadrat in Fig. 6 is the cheapest practical in the syllabus - four sticks and some string, or a square bent out of wire. Twenty minutes on the school field, with pairs throwing their own quadrat, fixes Q14 and Q15 permanently, and it is the sort of question BECE sets almost every year.
- Note on Q5: 2 water and 4 stones are straightforward, but pupils sometimes put 7 temperature with the living things because 'it changes'. Temperature is not alive - it does not feed, grow, respire or reproduce. If a pupil is unsure, ask them to run those four tests on it.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**12.1  12.1 Forms of Electricity Generation**

- **Q1** (4 marks) HYDRO: the potential energy of water held behind the dam changes to kinetic energy as it falls, then to electrical energy in the generator. SOLAR: light energy from the sun changes straight to electrical energy. WIND: the kinetic energy of moving air turns the turbine, changing to electrical energy. THERMAL: the chemical energy in the fuel is released as heat by burning, the heat boils water to make steam, the steam turns the turbine, and the generator changes it to electrical energy.
- **Q2** (3 marks) A hydro dam depends on water held behind it. In a long dry season the river runs low and the reservoir falls, so the dam cannot turn its turbines and generation stops. Solar would be more reliable through the dry season, because the dry season is also the sunniest time of year - the resource is greatest exactly when the dam's is least.

**12.2  12.2 Impact on the Environment**

- **Q3** (3 marks) The dam floods the land behind it, which changes the river's flow and the plants and animals living in it. Water released from the bottom of the reservoir is cold and low in oxygen, which harms fish downstream. Warm water poured back in after cooling the plant raises the river's temperature, which also harms the organisms living in it.
- **Q4** (3 marks) Any two reasons: the smoke from burning the fuel pollutes the air and causes breathing problems; the plant gives out gases that add to climate change; the ash has to be dumped somewhere and spoils the land. One way to reduce it: fit filters or scrubbers to the chimneys to take the smoke and harmful gases out before they reach the air, or use a cleaner fuel such as gas instead of coal or oil.

**12.3  12.3 Basic Electronic Components**

- **Q5** (3 marks) The rectangle is a resistor. The triangle with a bar is a diode. The circle with an A is an ammeter, which measures current.
- **Q6** (3 marks) In the OPEN position there is a gap in the circuit, so the path is broken and NO current flows. In the CLOSED position the gap is bridged, the circuit is complete, and current flows all the way round.
- **Q7** (3 marks) An LED only needs a very small current, and it has almost no resistance of its own. Without a resistor to limit the current, far too much would flow through the LED, it would overheat and it would be destroyed - it would burn out.

**12.4  12.4 Assembling a Simple Circuit**

- **Q8** (4 marks) The other bulb goes out. In a series circuit there is only ONE loop, so the current has only one path. Unscrewing one bulb breaks that path, the circuit is no longer complete, and current stops everywhere in the circuit - including at the other bulb.
- **Q9** (3 marks) The other bulbs stay lit, as brightly as before. In a parallel circuit each bulb is on its own branch, so each has its own separate path back to the battery. Removing one branch does not break the others, so current still flows through them.
- **Q10** (4 marks) Two reasons: each lamp or appliance can be switched on and off on its own, because breaking one branch does not stop the others - in series, switching one lamp off would put out every lamp in the house. And each appliance gets the full voltage of the supply, so they all work properly - in series the voltage would be shared out and each one would be dim or weak.

**12.5  12.5 The P-N Junction Diode**

- **Q11** (4 marks) It lights in circuit A. The diode acts like a one-way valve: it lets current through in the direction its arrow points, and blocks it in the other direction. In A the diode is turned so its arrow points the same way the current is trying to go - this is FORWARD BIAS, so current flows and the bulb lights. In B the diode is turned the other way round - REVERSE BIAS - so it blocks the current, the circuit is effectively broken, and the bulb stays dark.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Forward bias means the diode is connected the right way round in the circuit, so that the current is trying to flow in the direction the diode allows - the direction its arrow points. The diode conducts and current flows.

**12.6  12.6 Functions and Interdependence**

- **Q13** (3 marks) SOURCE (the battery or generator) pushes the current round the circuit. CONDUCTOR (the copper wires) carries the current from one part to another. CONTROL (the switch) turns the current on and off. LOAD (the bulb, iron or radio) is the part that uses the electrical energy and does the job.
- **Q14** (3 marks) The conductor is what carries the current all the way round from the source, through the load, and back again. A break anywhere in that path leaves a gap, so the circuit is no longer a complete loop and current cannot flow at all. Because the same current has to pass through every part of the loop, one break stops it everywhere.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q15** (4 marks) Any two with a test: THE BREAK IN THE WIRE marked X - replace that piece of wire, or test it by connecting a known-good wire across the gap and seeing if the lamp lights. A FLAT CELL - swap it for a fresh cell and see if the lamp lights. A BLOWN LAMP - swap it for a lamp known to work. A FAULTY SWITCH - connect the two wires together bypassing the switch. LOOSE CONNECTION - push each connection firm and see if the lamp flickers on.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 44% are Challenging.
- Q8 and Q9 are the pair the whole paper hangs on, and they are deliberately asked back to back. Pupils memorise 'in series they all go out, in parallel they stay on' without knowing why. The mark is for the REASON: series has one path, parallel has a separate branch for each bulb. Ask both, in that order, and the contrast teaches itself.
- Q10 is the payoff question - why houses are parallel. Pupils who have understood Q8 and Q9 answer it easily; pupils who only memorised the rule cannot. It is the best single test in the paper of whether the idea has landed.
- Q11 is the hardest. A diode is not intuitive, and the forward/reverse pair is exactly what BECE asks. The one sentence that unlocks it: the arrow on the diode symbol points the way current is ALLOWED to go. Say it, draw it, and test it with a real LED and a button cell - a diode that is the wrong way round is the commonest reason a pupil's first circuit fails.
- Q2 is the Applied question most pupils get wrong. They pick solar because it is 'modern' or 'clean' and lose the marks. The reasoning is about WHEN each resource is available: the dry season is the sunniest time and the worst time for a dam. Reward any answer that reasons about the timing of the resource.
- Q7 (the resistor and the LED) is beyond what most B7 classes meet in lessons, but it is the standard reason a real LED circuit burns out, and it is worth the three marks. If your class has not met LEDs, treat it as extension.
- Fig. 7 is the cheapest practical in the paper and the one to actually do: give pairs a battery, a bulb, a switch and three wires, then cut one wire and let them find the fault. Ten minutes of that makes Q15 automatic, and fault-finding is a skill BECE tests repeatedly.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**11.1  11.1 What is Energy?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Energy is the ability to do work. The raised stone has stored, or potential, energy because of its position above the ground - work was done against gravity to lift it there, and that work is now stored in it. Nothing appears to be happening because the energy is stored and not yet being used, but if the stone is released it will fall, and as it falls it can do work - it can drive a nail in or break something. Energy is the ability to do work, and the stone has that ability waiting.
- **Q2** (2 marks) Any two, each with a correct example: chemical - energy stored in food, fuel or a battery; heat - from a fire or a hot iron; light - from a lit bulb or the sun; sound - from a drum or a radio; electrical - carried by the current in a wire; mechanical - a moving car or a falling stone; nuclear - released in a reactor; solar - sunlight falling on a panel.

**11.2  11.2 Forms of Energy**

- **Q3** (3 marks) A battery stores CHEMICAL energy, not electrical energy. The chemicals inside it react when it is connected in a circuit, and that reaction drives the current - so the battery is a store of chemical energy which is changed into electrical energy as it is used. The correction matters because the change happens at a particular point: the chemical energy is there whether or not the battery is connected, and it only becomes electrical once a circuit is made. The other forms in the diagram are the same - each is a form the energy takes at a particular stage.

**11.3  11.3 Potential and Kinetic Energy**

- **Q4** (4 marks) At A the bob is high and momentarily still, so its energy is almost all potential. As it swings down towards B gravity pulls it and it loses height, so its potential energy falls. That lost potential energy does not disappear - it is changed into kinetic energy, the energy of movement. B is the lowest point of the swing, so by the time the bob reaches B the greatest possible amount of energy has been changed into kinetic energy, and kinetic energy depends on speed. So the bob is moving fastest at B.
- **Q5** (3 marks) The energy has been changed into heat and sound, spread out into the air and into the pivot where the pendulum rubs. It has not been destroyed, so the total energy is still exactly the same - energy is conserved. It has simply been changed into forms that are spread so thinly and are so useless to us that the pendulum can no longer swing with them, which is why the motion dies away. The energy is still there; it has just become unavailable.

**11.4  11.4 Calculating PE and KE**

- **Q6** (4 marks) The last column shows that PE plus KE is 400 J at every height - it never changes. That is the point: as the stone falls, energy is not created as it speeds up and not destroyed as it loses height. It is only changed from one form into the other, with the total staying exactly the same throughout. This is what conservation of energy means - the total amount of energy in a closed system stays constant, and all that can happen is that it changes form.
- **Q7** (3 marks) The pupil has added the same energy up twice. The 400 J of kinetic energy at the bottom is not new energy - it is the very same 400 J that was potential energy at the top, changed into another form. The table shows there is never more than 400 J at any one moment: the last column is 400 throughout, not 800. Energy is conserved, which means it can only be changed from one form to another, never created.

**11.5  11.5 Daily Applications of Energy**

- **Q8** (3 marks) Chemical energy in the battery is changed into light energy, with some heat as well. A flat battery has run out of the chemicals that react to produce the current, so its store of chemical energy is used up. With no energy going into the torch, none can come out of it as light. The torch is only a converter - it cannot produce light without an energy input.
- **Q9** (3 marks) It is wasted because the bulb's job is to give light, and the heat is an unwanted by-product that does nothing useful - the energy going into it is not being used for the purpose the bulb was made for. Any sensible suggestion: use an LED or a fluorescent lamp instead, which produces far less heat for the same amount of light and so wastes less energy; or switch the lamp off when it is not needed.

**11.6  11.6 Heat Transfer**

- **Q10** (3 marks) Radiation. The diagram shows heat from the sun reaching you, and between the sun and the earth there is almost entirely empty space - there is no solid, liquid or gas in between to carry it. Conduction needs a solid and convection needs a liquid or a gas, so neither could do it. Radiation travels as infrared waves, which need no material at all.
- **Q11** (4 marks) When the water at the bottom is heated its particles gain energy and move about more vigorously, so they push each other further apart. That means the same mass of water now takes up more space - it has expanded and become less dense than the colder water around it. Being less dense, it floats up through the colder, denser water, which sinks down to take its place at the bottom. That colder water is then heated in turn, and the circulation goes on as a convection current.

**11.7  11.7 Characteristics of Light**

- **Q12** (3 marks) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection - the incoming ray and the reflected ray make equal angles with the normal. The dashed line is the NORMAL, a line drawn at right angles to the mirror at the point where the ray strikes it. It is needed because both angles are measured from it, not from the surface of the mirror - without it there is nothing to measure the angles against.
- **Q13** (4 marks) This is refraction. Light coming from the part of the stick under the water leaves the water and enters the air, and as it crosses from water into air it changes speed and bends away from the normal. Our eyes and brain always assume light has travelled in a straight line, so they trace the bent rays straight back and place the underwater part of the stick higher than it really is. That is why the stick looks bent, or broken, at the water surface.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q14** (4 marks) The copper rod, because copper is the best conductor of the four and so carries the heat along to the wax fastest, melting it first - as the table shows, its pin drops in 48 s. The order tells you the ranking of the rods as conductors: the sooner the pin drops, the better that material conducts heat. So copper conducts better than aluminium, aluminium better than iron, and iron conducts while wood effectively does not conduct at all.
- **Q15** (3 marks) The wax melts at a fixed temperature, so it gives a fair, measurable signal - the pin drops at the moment the end of that rod reaches the same temperature in every case. Feeling the rods with your hand is unreliable: it is a judgement that varies from person to person, it cannot be timed, and it would burn you. Using wax makes the test the same for every rod and lets you time it, so the results can be compared.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 78% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is where the 'energy is the ability to do work' definition is usually parroted and then abandoned. The mark for the second half comes from saying the raised stone has work stored IN it because work was done to lift it, and that this waiting ability becomes real the moment it is released.
- Q7 is the best diagnostic in the paper. Half a class will add 400 and 400 and get 800, and say energy has been created. They have counted the same energy twice. The cure is the last column of Fig. 4: it is 400 at every single height, so there was never any question of 800.
- Q5 and Q6 are the pair that does the real work on conservation. Q5 is the honest case - a pendulum really does stop - and the answer is that the energy went to heat and sound and is now too spread out to use. Pupils who can hold both of these at once have the idea.
- Q4 on why the bob is fastest at B is a four-mark chain: height goes down, PE goes down, PE becomes KE, KE means speed. Mark the chain, not the conclusion - pupils who simply write 'because it is at the bottom' have skipped all four links.
- Q13 on the bent stick needs both halves: the rays bend away from the normal leaving the water, AND the brain assumes straight lines. Most pupils give only the first and score two of four.
- The conduction practical in Fig. 8 is cheap to run - four rods, a block, drawing pins and wax - and it gives a genuine ranking with a genuine timing. If you want a third practical question, ask for two fair-test variables (same length, same thickness, same mass of wax, same size of pin); both length and thickness change the time independently of the material, so both must be controlled.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**10.1  10.1 Types of Farming Systems in Ghana**

- **Q1** (4 marks) For the Northern Region farmer: land rotation. It asks little of each hectare - the plot is cropped, then abandoned to recover by itself while the family moves on - so a small workforce can still farm a large area, and there is land to spare. For the Kumasi farmer: mixed cropping, ideally within an organic system. Land is scarce and expensive, so the aim is to get as much as possible off every square metre; mixed cropping gives two harvests from the same ground, and the large family supplies the labour it needs for careful planting, weeding and composting. The nearby town also provides a market that will pay more for organic produce. Nothing about land rotation would suit him: he has no spare land to rotate onto.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: land rotation, crop rotation, mixed cropping, mixed farming, organic farming.

**10.2  10.2 Land Rotation Farming**

- **Q3** (4 marks) While a plot lies fallow, wild plants grow on it and die back, and their remains rot into humus, replacing the nutrients the crop removed; the soil structure recovers as roots and soil organisms work through it, and any pest or disease specific to the cropped plant dies out for want of a host. The system only works, though, on two conditions: that there is always more land to move to, and that each plot is left long enough - usually several years - to recover properly. As a village grows, spare land disappears and the fallow period has to be cut short. Plots go back into cultivation before they have recovered, yields fall, and the system collapses into continuous cropping on exhausted ground. That is why it is now rare in the densely farmed parts of southern Ghana.

**10.3  10.3 Crop Rotation Farming**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Maize is a heavy feeder, particularly of nitrogen, so a maize crop takes a great deal out of the soil and leaves it poorer. Groundnuts are legumes, and legumes carry nodules on their roots containing bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, so a groundnut crop puts nitrogen back rather than taking it out. Placing the groundnut between the two maize crops restores what the first maize crop removed, so the second maize crop finds the nitrogen it needs. There is a second benefit: pests and diseases specific to maize cannot survive a season without maize to live on, so the break in the sequence reduces their build-up - which continuous maize cannot do.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. Different crops take different nutrients, so no single nutrient is drained season after season. A legume in the sequence puts nitrogen back into the soil. It breaks the life cycle of pests and diseases specific to one crop. A deep-rooted crop following a shallow-rooted one opens up the soil and reaches food lower down. It reduces the need to buy fertiliser.

**10.4  10.4 Mixed Cropping**

- **Q6** (4 marks) How the beans help: first, they are legumes, so the bacteria in their root nodules fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, and the maize can use it. Second, the bean plants spread across the ground between the maize rows and shade it, so fewer weeds can establish and the soil loses less water by evaporation. How they might harm each other: both are growing on the same ground at the same time, so they compete for water and for the same nutrients - nitrogen above all, if the beans are not fixing enough to spare. A climbing bean may also pull the maize stems over, and dense bean growth can shade young maize plants too heavily.
- **Q7** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. It gives two harvests from the same piece of land instead of one. It spreads the risk: if one crop fails, the other may still do well. The ground cover reduces weeds and protects the soil from erosion. A legume partner feeds the other crop.

**10.5  10.5 Mixed Farming**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Animals depending on crops, any two: crop residues such as maize stover, cassava leaves and groundnut haulms are fed to them; grain and cassava tubers are fed to pigs and poultry; the animals are grazed on the stubble and weeds left after harvest. Crops depending on animals, any two: their dung and urine are collected and spread on the fields as manure; their droppings go into the compost pit; grazing animals clear the weeds and stubble and their hooves work crop residue into the ground; where oxen are used they supply the power to plough.
- **Q9** (3 marks) A farm on which crops are grown and animals are kept at the same time, and where the two are deliberately linked rather than merely side by side: the crop waste and residues feed the animals, and the animal dung and urine are returned to the land to feed the next crop.

**10.6  10.6 Organic Farming**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Organic farming uses no synthetic fertiliser, so every nutrient the crop takes up has to be released by the decay of organic matter. The compost pit is where that decay is managed: it turns crop waste and dung into humus, which releases its nutrients slowly and also improves the structure and water-holding of the soil. Without it the farm has no nutrient supply at all. Yields are lower at first because the soil has been accustomed to fertiliser that delivers nutrients quickly and in quantity, whereas compost releases them gradually and in smaller amounts. The soil's structure, its water-holding and its population of organisms all take several seasons to build up. Over time the gap narrows and the soil is in better heart than before.
- **Q11** (3 marks) The green waste is soft, moist and rich in nitrogen, which the micro-organisms need to build their bodies and multiply. The dry straw and leaves are rich in carbon and hold the heap open so that air can circulate and the mass does not collapse into a slimy, smelly, airless lump. Too much of either and the heap either rots badly or barely rots at all. Turning it over mixes the two materials, lets fresh air into the middle so the decomposers can respire, and stops the outside drying out while the inside goes short of oxygen.

**10.7  10.7 Merits and Demerits of Each Farming System**

- **Q12** (3 marks) Organic farming, using mixed cropping within it. The plot is small, so a somewhat lower yield per hectare matters less than the cost of the inputs; the large family supplies the labour that organic farming demands for composting, weeding and hand control of pests; and the nearby town provides a market that will pay a premium for organic produce, which makes up for the smaller harvest. Having little money for chemicals is no obstacle, because none are bought. Mixed cropping suits the small area for the same reason - it gets two harvests off the same ground.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (3 marks) Plot A grew maize in all three seasons. Maize takes a great deal of nitrogen and other nutrients out of the soil, and nothing was put back, so the soil was drained a little more each season - which is exactly what the figures show: 2 400 kg, then 1 850 kg, then 1 300 kg, a loss of nearly half in three seasons. In plot B the beans of year two were legumes, so their root nodules put nitrogen back into the soil instead of taking it out, and they were not maize, so the pests and diseases of maize had no host for a season. When maize was planted again in year three the soil still had what it needed, so the yield held at 2 260 kg. The beans were not weighed as maize, but their effect shows up clearly in the maize crop that followed them.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Both plots must be the same size and on the same type of soil - otherwise the difference in yield could be due to the plot rather than to the rotation. The same maize variety must be used, planted at the same spacing and on the same date. Both plots must receive the same watering and weeding. The grain must be harvested and dried the same way before weighing - if one plot's grain is weighed while still damp it will weigh more and the comparison will be worthless.
- **Q15** (2 marks) The amount of the crop harvested from a given area of land - for example, the mass of grain in kilograms obtained from one hectare.

- Q3 on land rotation is the one that separates a description from an explanation. Almost every pupil can say 'the farmer moves to another plot'. Very few can say what the fallow actually DOES - wild growth rots into humus, the structure recovers, the crop-specific pests starve. Push them on the second half too: the system needs spare land, and once the village grows it has none.
- Q4 on the groundnut between two maize crops is the paper's best question. The mechanism is nitrogen fixation by the legume's root nodules, and it is worth naming the nodules. The second mark, on breaking the pest cycle, is the one that is usually missed - rotation helps for two separate reasons, not one.
- Q6 asks pupils to argue both ways, which is harder than it looks. They will list the benefits of the beans happily and then insist there is no downside. There is: two crops on one piece of ground are competing for the same water and nutrients. A farmer who cannot see that will over-plant.
- Q10 is the question that justifies the whole 10.6 strand. Organic farming is not 'farming without chemicals' - it is farming where the nutrient supply has been replaced by a compost pit. If the pit is not managed, the farm has no nutrients at all. The lower early yields follow from the same fact: compost releases slowly, fertiliser does not.
- The rotation experiment in Fig. 8 needs two plots and three seasons, which is more than one class can usually manage. If time is short, run it as a demonstration started by a previous year group, or use the school farm's own records. The numbers are representative rather than real, and it is worth saying so to the class.
- Q15 on the meaning of yield looks trivial and is not. Pupils routinely confuse the yield of a crop with the size of an individual plant, and then wonder why a plot of stunted-looking plants out-yields a plot of tall ones.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**14.1  14.1 What is Force?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) (a) Non-contact. The magnet and the compass needle never touch - the magnet acts through the air and the case by its magnetic field. (b) Contact. Friction only arises where the sole of the foot and the surface of the tile are actually pressed together and rubbing. (c) Non-contact. Gravity pulls the coconut down through the air all the way to the ground with nothing touching it; it acts through the earth's gravitational field. (d) Contact. The blade has to be pushed right against the earth before it can push it - the force disappears the moment the blade is lifted clear.
- **Q2** (3 marks) A force is a push or a pull acting on an object; it can change the object's motion or its shape. Any two named forces: muscular (frictional), friction, gravitational (weight), magnetic, electrostatic, upthrust, tension.

**14.2  14.2 Balanced and Unbalanced Forces**

- **Q3** (3 marks) 1. It STOPS the ball - the ball was moving and the force from his gloves brings it to rest. 2. It CHANGES THE DIRECTION of the ball - if he palms it away rather than holding it, the force deflects it along a new path. 3. It CHANGES THE SHAPE of the ball - the ball squashes against his gloves for the moment of the catch, then springs back. All three come from the same single blow, which is the point the diagram makes.

**14.3  14.3 Inertia**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Where it helps - walking. To move forward you push backwards against the ground with your foot. Friction opposes the tendency of your foot to slide backwards, so it gives you something to push against and you move forward. On a wet or polished floor there is little friction, your foot slides, and you cannot walk properly. Where it wastes - the bearings in a bicycle wheel or a car engine. The metal surfaces rub as they turn, friction opposes the turning, and the work done against it is converted into heat. Energy that came from the rider's muscles or from the fuel ends up warming the bearings instead of moving the machine. That is why bearings are greased, and why they wear out and have to be replaced.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Reducing, any two: put oil or grease between the surfaces; use wheels, rollers or ball bearings so the surfaces roll instead of sliding; make the surfaces smoother; separate them with a cushion of air as a hovercraft does. Increasing, any two: make the surfaces rougher, as with sandpaper or a tyre tread; press the surfaces together harder, as a heavier load does; use a material that grips more, such as rubber.

**14.4  14.4 Newton's First Law of Motion**

- **Q6** (4 marks) The two forces on the book are equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cancel each other: the resultant force on the book is zero. A resultant of zero means no change in motion, so the book stays exactly as it is - at rest. It is not that no forces act on it; two do. It is that together they add to nothing. Take the table away and the upward push disappears. The forces are now unbalanced: 6 N downwards with nothing opposing it. The book therefore accelerates downwards - it falls, and it goes faster the longer it falls.
- **Q7** (3 marks) The resultant is 800 N - 800 N = 0 N. The pulls are equal and opposite, so they cancel and the rope stays at rest. When team A begins to win, their pull has become greater than team B's. The forces are now unbalanced, there is a resultant in A's direction, and the rope accelerates towards team A. It is not that team B has stopped pulling - B's pull is simply now the smaller of the two.

**14.5  14.5 Applications of Newton's First Law**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Acceleration is a change in velocity, and velocity is not the same thing as speed: velocity includes the direction of motion. The stone's speed is constant, but its direction is changing at every instant, because to stay on the circle it must be turning all the time. So its velocity is continually changing, and therefore it is accelerating - even though nothing about the speed changes. Because the direction turns towards the centre, the acceleration is towards the centre, and so there must be a resultant force towards the centre. Here that force is the tension in the string, pulling inward along its length. Cut the string and the force vanishes; the stone then stops turning and goes straight on along the tangent, which is exactly what the diagram shows.

**14.6  14.6 Magnets: Types and Characteristics**

- **Q9** (4 marks) Nothing is pushing her to the right. Before the turn, she and the bus are both moving straight ahead. As the bus turns left, the floor and whatever she is holding push on her and turn her left too - that inward push is the centripetal force, and it is what makes her follow the curve instead of continuing straight. But her body tends, by inertia, to keep going in the original straight line, so relative to the turning bus she drifts towards the right-hand side and ends up pressed against it. What she feels as an outward 'centrifugal force' is simply her own body trying to carry straight on while the bus turns underneath her. The real force on her is inward, towards the centre of the turn - the outward feeling is an effect of her own inertia, not a force at all.
- **Q10** (3 marks) A centripetal force is a REAL force acting towards the centre of the circle - the tension in a string, the pull of gravity, or the grip of tyres on a road - and it is what keeps an object moving in a circle instead of going straight. The centrifugal force is NOT a real force at all: it is the apparent outward effect you feel because your body tends to keep moving in a straight line while whatever is carrying you turns inward beneath you.

**14.7  14.7 Repulsion, Attraction and Orientation**

- **Q11** (3 marks) The drum spins the clothes round in a circle at high speed. To keep something moving in a circle there must be a force pulling it inward, and for the clothes that force comes from the drum wall pushing on them. But the water in the cloth is only loosely held, and the drum has holes in it, so the wall cannot push on the water. With no inward force to hold it in the circle, the water simply continues in a straight line - out through the holes and into the outer casing. The faster the drum spins, the greater the inward force the water would need, and so the more of it is thrown out.

**14.8  14.8 Uses of Magnets**

- **Q12** (3 marks) It is falling - continuously. Gravity is the inward force that bends its path, and it never stops acting on the satellite. But the satellite also has a very large sideways speed, and as it falls towards the earth the earth's surface curves away beneath it at just the same rate, so the satellite keeps missing the ground. Gravity curves its path into a closed loop around the earth rather than letting it fly off in a straight line, and with no air up there to slow it down it keeps its speed. An orbit is a permanent fall that never lands.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (3 marks) 1. A rougher surface gives more friction. With no load on the block, the bare bench gives 2.0 N but sandpaper gives 4.6 N - more than twice as much for the same block and the same load. Oiling the bench cuts it to 1.1 N, which is lower than the bare bench. 2. A heavier load gives more friction. On the bare bench the reading rises from 2.0 N with no load to 3.1 N with 1 kg on top and 4.3 N with 2 kg - roughly doubling as the load goes up. A third conclusion: rollers almost remove friction entirely, cutting the reading from 2.0 N to 0.3 N.
- **Q14** (3 marks) If the block is moving at a steady speed its motion is not changing, so the forces on it must be balanced: the pull forwards is exactly equal to the friction backwards, and the balance reading therefore IS the friction. If the block were accelerating, the forces would no longer be balanced - the pull would have to be greater than the friction in order to produce the acceleration. The reading would then be higher than the true friction, and it would not settle to a steady value because the block would keep gaining speed.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. The same block must be used, pulled on the same face, so that the area in contact is the same in every trial. The pull must be horizontal in each case - if the balance is tilted, part of the pull goes into lifting the block rather than overcoming friction, and the reading is not the friction. The same load must be used when comparing one surface with another. The balance should be checked to read zero before each trial, and read at eye level to avoid a parallax error.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q8 is the best question here, and the one that decides whether a pupil understands circular motion or has merely memorised the word. The whole answer hangs on one distinction: speed is how fast, velocity is how fast AND which way. A stone on a string has constant speed and constantly changing velocity, so it is accelerating. Pupils who say 'its speed is constant so there is no acceleration' have the wrong definition, not a missing fact.
- Q9 on the turning bus is the same idea from inside. Nothing pushes the passenger outwards. She keeps going straight; the bus turns in underneath her. If a pupil finishes the answer still believing a centrifugal force pushed her, they have not got it - and this is the single most common misconception in the whole strand.
- Q12 on the satellite is worth doing aloud at the board. 'It is falling and missing' is the sentence to aim for; it is short, it is correct, and it is memorable in a way that 'gravity is balanced by centrifugal force' is not - that answer is wrong and very common.
- Q4 on friction both helping and wasting is where pupils show whether they can argue both sides. Most can give one example of friction being a nuisance (wearing out soles) but cannot say what it does when it helps, which is: give you something to push against.
- The friction experiment needs a spring balance reading to at least 0.1 N, a wooden block with a hook, and a set of masses. Reading the balance while the block is actually moving at a steady speed is the awkward part - a slow, steady pull takes practice, and it is worth letting each group have several attempts before recording.
- If spring balances are short, the whole class can work from one balance passed round, or the four surfaces can be tested by different groups and the results pooled on the board.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**17.1  17.1 Food Nutrients and the Human Body**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Plain rice is almost entirely carbohydrate, so it supplies energy and very little else. It gives the child the fuel to move and keep warm, but almost no protein for growth and repair, very little fat, and only traces of the vitamins and minerals the body needs - especially if the rice is well milled, which strips off the bran and germ where most of the B vitamins are. So the child may be full, and may even be taking in enough energy, yet still lack the protein to build muscle and blood, the vitamin A to keep the eyes and the lining of the gut healthy, and the iron to avoid anaemia. Malnutrition is not the same as hunger: it is a shortage of the RIGHT things, and a large plate of one single food cannot supply all seven nutrients. That is why the condition is called a deficiency rather than starvation - and why a child can look fed and still be ill.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals, water, roughage (fibre).
- **Q3** (3 marks) Gari is made from cassava and is mainly carbohydrate - it supplies the energy. Beans are mainly protein - they supply the material for growth and repair. Together the meal supplies both energy and body-building material, and the beans add fibre, iron and some B vitamins as well. Gari alone would fill the pupil up and supply energy, but would give almost no protein, so the body would have the fuel it needs and none of the material to grow on. The beans supply exactly what the gari lacks, which is the point of combining a staple with a legume.
- **Q4** (3 marks) Carbohydrate: the body's main source of energy, released by respiration. Protein: growth and repair of tissues, and for making enzymes, some hormones and haemoglobin. Roughage (fibre): it gives the gut bulk, so that the muscles of the intestine have something to push against and can move food along - without it, constipation results.

**17.2  17.2 Deficiency Diseases: Causes, Symptoms, Effects and Prevention**

- **Q5** (4 marks) A balanced diet contains all seven nutrients in the right proportions and in enough quantity: sufficient energy for the work the body does, enough protein for growth and repair, and enough of each vitamin and mineral. It must also be varied, because no single food contains everything. The labourer is doing heavy physical work all day, so his muscles are respiring far harder and he needs substantially more carbohydrate and fat than the office worker. The office worker, sitting for most of the day, needs much less; if he ate the labourer's plate he would store the surplus as fat and put on weight. Their protein, vitamin and mineral needs, however, are about the same, because those depend on body size and on repair rather than on how much physical work is done.
- **Q6** (3 marks) About 45% of the plate should be the staple - rice, yam, cassava, plantain or maize - since that is where the carbohydrate comes from. About 30% should be vegetables and fruit, supplying vitamins, minerals and fibre. About 15% should be a protein food such as fish, meat, eggs, beans or groundnuts, and about 10% fat or oil. The staple is the largest part because energy is what the body uses most of, and carbohydrate is the cheapest and most straightforward way to supply it. Turning the plate round - mostly meat - would be expensive, would not supply enough energy, and would leave the body short of the fuel it needs most.
- **Q7** (3 marks) Any two, each stated. No single food contains all seven nutrients, so eating only one means some are missing altogether. Even where a nutrient is present, the proportions are wrong: one is supplied in great excess while others are absent, and excess can be as harmful as shortage. It also allows no variety, and a diet built on one food is monotonous enough that people eat less of it. Health depends on eating a range of foods.

**17.3  17.3 Night Blindness, Rickets, Scurvy, Kwashiorkor and Anaemia**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Kwashiorkor is a deficiency of PROTEIN, not of food in general. A child may be getting a full belly of a starchy staple - maize porridge, rice, cassava - and so be taking in enough energy, while getting almost no protein at all. Without protein the liver cannot make enough albumin, the protein that holds water inside the blood vessels, so fluid leaks out into the tissues and the belly swells; and the body cannot build new tissue, so growth stops and the hair and skin break down. It appears just after weaning because up to that point the child was getting its protein from breast milk, and the food that replaces it is usually a thin starchy gruel with almost none. The child is still being fed - but the one source of protein has been taken away and replaced by starch, and the deficiency shows within weeks.
- **Q9** (4 marks) The first child has iron-deficiency ANAEMIA. Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen, so without it the blood cannot deliver enough oxygen to the muscles: hence the pallor, the tiredness and the breathlessness. Foods to correct it: liver, red meat, dark green leafy vegetables, beans, groundnuts, and iron-fortified foods. The second child has vitamin A deficiency causing NIGHT BLINDNESS. Vitamin A is needed to make the light-sensitive pigment in the retina that works when light is dim, so without it vision fails at dusk. Foods to correct it: red palm oil, liver, egg yolk, dark green leaves, orange-fleshed sweet potato, mango, pawpaw.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Beriberi is caused by a lack of vitamin B1, thiamine. Thiamine is concentrated in the bran and the germ of the rice grain, and both are removed when rice is milled white. So a diet built on well-milled rice can supply plenty of energy and still contain almost no vitamin B1. The remedy is to eat unrefined or parboiled rice instead, or to add other sources of thiamine to the diet - whole grains, unrefined flour, groundnuts, beans. Parboiling before milling drives the vitamin out of the husk and into the grain itself, which is why parboiled rice does not cause beriberi.
- **Q11** (3 marks) A deficiency disease is an illness caused by the lack of a particular nutrient in the diet over a period of time. It is not caused by a germ and cannot be caught from another person; it is corrected by supplying the missing nutrient. Any two examples: kwashiorkor (protein), marasmus (overall energy), night blindness (vitamin A), beriberi (vitamin B1), scurvy (vitamin C), rickets (vitamin D), anaemia (iron), goitre (iodine).

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q12** (4 marks) Cooked rice went blue-black with iodine and gave no change with either of the other two, so it contains starch and no detectable reducing sugar or protein - which is what you would expect of a staple grain, since plants store their surplus energy as starch. Milk went violet with Biuret, so it contains protein, and gave a pale orange with Benedict's, so it also contains a reducing sugar - the lactose that milk naturally contains. So a single food can test positive for several nutrients at once, and each reagent answers a separate question: iodine asks whether starch is present, Benedict's whether a reducing sugar is present, Biuret whether protein is present. The three tests are independent, and a result with one tells you nothing about the other two.
- **Q13** (3 marks) The control is a tube containing water in place of the food, treated with exactly the same reagent and heated in exactly the same way for the same time. It shows what a negative result looks like - that is, the colour the reagent is to begin with. Without it a pupil cannot tell whether the colour they see comes from the food or is simply the reagent's own colour: Benedict's solution is blue and iodine solution is brown, and either could easily be misread as a positive result. The control should show no change: iodine staying orange-brown, Benedict's staying blue after heating, Biuret staying blue.
- **Q14** (3 marks) She must first check that the test was carried out properly - in particular that she added Benedict's solution AND then heated the tube in a water bath for several minutes. Benedict's reagent only gives its brick-red colour on heating; without it, the tube stays blue whatever the food contains. She should also compare the tube against the water control, and ideally repeat the test. Only then can she conclude that no reducing sugar is present. If she forgot the heating, the negative result means nothing at all, because the reagent was never given the conditions it needs to react.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Wear eye protection: iodine, Biuret reagent and hot Benedict's solution all damage the eye. Heat the Benedict's tube in a water bath rather than straight over a flame, because the solution spits and can throw hot liquid into the face. Wash off at once any iodine or Biuret that touches the skin and tell the teacher - iodine stains and irritates, and Biuret contains sodium hydroxide, which burns. Tie back long hair and stand up while heating, and point the mouth of the tube away from everyone.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 and Q8 are the pair that carry this paper, and they are the same argument at two levels. A child can be full and still be malnourished. A child can be weaned onto a bellyful of maize porridge and develop kwashiorkor, because the porridge has energy and no protein. The sentence worth drilling is 'malnutrition is not the same as hunger'. Pupils who get this have understood the difference between energy and body-building material, which is what the whole of 17.1 and 17.3 is about.
- Q8's second half is the one that earns the fourth mark. Kwashiorkor appears at weaning not because the child stops being fed, but because breast milk - the protein source - is replaced by starch. Almost nobody says this unprompted, and it is the difference between a description and an explanation.
- Q10 on beriberi and milled rice is a piece of genuine history that pupils find surprising: a diet can be adequate in energy and still kill, because milling removes the part of the grain that carries the vitamin.
- For the food tests you need iodine solution, Benedict's solution, Biuret (or sodium hydroxide plus copper sulphate), a water bath, and test-tube holders. Solid foods should be crushed with a little water first. The most common error by far is forgetting to heat the Benedict's tube - Q14 is aimed straight at it.
- Benedict's and Biuret can be hard to get in some schools. Iodine is usually available from a pharmacy as tincture of iodine diluted; if you can only run one test, run the starch test, and tell the class honestly that the other two are being described rather than done.
- The milk result in Fig. 4 is the most interesting row in the table, because milk is positive for two nutrients. It is worth asking the class why, and whether they expected a food to test positive more than once.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**17.4  17.4 Nature of Viral Diseases**

- **Q1** (4 marks) HIV attacks the immune system itself - the very cells that coordinate the body's defences against everything else. Most viruses attack one organ and the body either clears them or keeps them in check: measles attacks the airways and skin, hepatitis B attacks the liver, and the immune system deals with them. HIV destroys the system that would do the dealing. So the person does not die of HIV as such. They die of infections that a healthy body would shrug off - tuberculosis, pneumonia, severe diarrhoea, certain cancers. What makes HIV serious is not what the virus does to any one organ but that it removes the body's ability to fight anything else. That is also why the illness is called a syndrome - AIDS - rather than a single disease: the eventual illness is different in different people.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B, measles, polio, rabies, chickenpox, yellow fever, the common cold.
- **Q3** (3 marks) The first child has MEASLES. The rash begins behind the ears and spreads downwards, and the virus attacks the airways and the skin. The second child has HEPATITIS B. The yellowing is jaundice, caused by the liver failing to clear bile pigment from the blood, and the virus attacks the liver. So in the first child the trouble is in the breathing passages and the skin, which is why the rash appears; in the second it is in the liver, which is why the eyes go yellow rather than the skin going blotchy.

**17.5  17.5 COVID-19: Causes, Symptoms, Transmission and Prevention**

- **Q4** (4 marks) To infect someone, a virus has to reach cells it can enter, in sufficient numbers, before it is destroyed. HIV is a fragile virus: it dries out and dies quickly in air, it is destroyed by stomach acid and digestive enzymes, and it can only enter through the bloodstream or through mucous membranes. Saliva, tears and sweat contain almost no virus, and sharing a cup delivers a trace amount into the mouth and then the stomach, where it is destroyed - so there is no route in and not enough virus anyway. Unbroken skin is a complete barrier, so a handshake cannot transmit it. A mosquito does not inject blood from the person it last bit; it injects saliva, and any virus in the blood it swallowed is digested - and HIV cannot multiply inside an insect in any case. A shared needle is different on every count: it carries blood, it injects that blood straight past the skin into the bloodstream, and the blood in the barrel is shielded from the air. So it is not that sharing needles is vaguely 'unhygienic' - it is that only that route delivers live virus past the skin in quantity.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. Through blood and body fluids - unsterilised needles, unscreened blood transfusions, unprotected sex. By droplets in the air from coughing, sneezing and talking in a crowded room. By the faeces-to-mouth route - dirty water, unwashed hands, flies landing on food. By a bite from an infected animal or insect - a dog with rabies, a mosquito carrying yellow fever.
- **Q6** (3 marks) Any three, each explained. Boil or treat the drinking water, so that any virus in it is destroyed before anyone drinks it. Build and use pit latrines, sited well away from the water source, so that faeces cannot reach the water or the food in the first place. Wash hands with soap after using the latrine and before handling food, so that virus picked up on the hands is not carried to the mouth. Keep food covered and screened from flies, which carry virus from faeces to food on their feet and mouthparts.

**17.6  17.6 Ebola and H1N1 Diseases**

- **Q7** (4 marks) A vaccine contains a harmless version of the virus, or a piece of it, which the immune system recognises as foreign. The body makes antibodies against it and, crucially, produces memory cells that persist for years. If the real virus later enters the body, those memory cells recognise it at once and produce antibodies fast enough to destroy it before it can establish an infection. This works for measles because the measles virus is stable: it has essentially one form, and the antibodies made against the vaccine virus recognise the real one perfectly well. HIV is different on two counts. It mutates extremely fast, so the surface the antibodies have learned to recognise has changed by the time the response is ready - the target keeps moving. And it attacks the very immune cells that would mount the response, so the defender is being destroyed while it works. Antiretroviral drugs control HIV by interfering with the virus's replication rather than by preventing infection.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Any three, each explained. Use a new, sterile, single-use needle and put it straight into a sharps box afterwards, so that no blood from one person can enter another. Wear gloves, so that any blood cannot reach cuts or grazes on her own hands. Cover any cuts or grazes on her hands with a waterproof dressing first, so that there is no route in. Screen every donation before transfusion, so that infected blood is never given to anyone. Clean up any spill with a disinfectant such as dilute bleach, which destroys the virus.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Screening means testing every donation of blood for the presence of particular viruses before the blood is used for a transfusion; any unit that tests positive is discarded. It prevents HIV and hepatitis B (and also hepatitis C and syphilis).

**17.7  17.7 Role of Individuals, Communities and Government**

- **Q10** (4 marks) Stigma drives the illness underground. If having HIV means losing your job, your friends and your place in the family, then the sensible thing for someone who suspects they may be infected is not to be tested. So they are not tested, they get no treatment, they change nothing, and they may pass the virus on for years without ever knowing they have it. Meanwhile everyone else, seeing what happened to the first person, avoids testing too. The result is that a preventable and now treatable infection keeps spreading in silence. Knowing the facts removes the reason for any of it. HIV is not spread by touching, by sharing food or cups, by a toilet seat, by saliva, tears or sweat, or by any insect. A family can therefore share meals, share a home, wash clothes and nurse a relative with HIV in complete safety. The only things that must not be shared are razors, toothbrushes and needles, and any cuts should be covered. And with antiretroviral treatment taken properly the virus becomes undetectable and cannot be passed on at all.
- **Q11** (3 marks) It is unnecessary because HIV is not spread by any of the things that sharing a home involves: not by sharing food or cups, not by touching or hugging, not by toilet seats, not by saliva, tears or sweat, and not by any insect. The virus needs blood or sexual fluids to get into another person's bloodstream, and none of that happens in ordinary family life. What the family should do instead: encourage him to attend the clinic and start antiretroviral treatment promptly, and support him to keep taking it; see that he eats well; and observe the one real precaution, which is not to share razors, toothbrushes or needles with him, and to keep any cuts covered. Beyond that he should be treated exactly as before - and the family can be tested themselves if that would set their minds at rest.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. With antiretroviral treatment taken properly, a person with HIV can live a long and working life. Taken properly, the drugs can make the virus undetectable in the blood, and at that point it cannot be passed on to anyone else. HIV is not spread by touching, by sharing food or cups, or by caring for someone. A person with HIV can marry, work, farm and have children who do not have the virus.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) The number rose quickly because each round of swaps multiplies the number of contacts. At the start one pupil out of five was 'infected'. After the first round of swaps still only one was - the exchanges simply had not happened to reach the right person. But after the second round, three of the five were positive, and by the third round all five were. Every exchange is an independent chance for the virus to move, so the total number of chances grows fast, and the number of people carrying it grows with it. And throughout, nobody could tell by looking which cups were positive: the liquid looked the same in every cup and the pupils behaved the same. That is precisely the point about a real infection. A person with HIV, or with hepatitis B, looks entirely well and feels entirely well, often for years. They do not know they have it, and neither does anyone else. No amount of looking tells you whether the person beside you is infected, and no amount of looking tells you whether you are. Only a test does. That is why the safe rule is to treat every exchange - every needle, every blade, every unscreened donation - as though it were a risk, rather than trusting appearances.
- **Q14** (3 marks) No real virus was used because this is a school. Even a harmless one would be irresponsible, and any virus that behaved the way HIV does would be dangerous. What is being modelled is not the virus but the PATTERN of spread - how many contacts, how quickly, and whether anyone can tell who is carrying it. The dilute sodium hydroxide in the 'infected' cup stands in for the virus: it is invisible in water, it passes from cup to cup exactly as a virus would, and it is revealed at the end by a colour change with the indicator. It could not be identified earlier because it is a colourless liquid in a colourless liquid. There is no visible sign - which is exactly the property being demonstrated. A person carrying a virus looks the same as everyone else.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two safety precautions, each explained. Wear eye protection, because the 'infected' liquid is dilute sodium hydroxide and splashes damage the eye. Wash hands at the end, and tell the teacher at once if any liquid touches the skin or the eyes. Do not drink from any cup or pipette, and put nothing in the mouth. For slowing the spread, any one with an explanation: reduce the number of exchanges - let each pupil swap with only one other per round instead of two, so there are fewer chances for the virus to move. Or 'screen' before swapping: test every cup and withdraw any that is positive, which is what screening donated blood does. Or have some pupils decline to swap at all, which is what vaccination, or never sharing a needle, does - fewer people who can catch it means the chain runs out of links.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the paper's central question and the one pupils most want answered. The answer is that HIV is serious not because of what it does to an organ but because it dismantles the system that defends every organ. Pupils who say 'it causes AIDS' have given a label, not an explanation.
- Q4 on why a handshake is safe but a shared needle is not is worth the full four marks of class time. It is not enough to say 'HIV is not spread by touching' - the pupil has to say why, which means explaining what the virus needs: a route past the skin, enough of it, and cells it can enter. Once that is clear, the whole list of myths falls over by itself.
- Q7 on why there is no HIV vaccine is the hardest question here and the most rewarding. The virus mutates faster than the immune response can be trained, and it attacks the cells that would do the training. Both reasons matter.
- Q10 and Q11 are the reason 17.7 exists. Stigma is not a matter of manners - it is the mechanism by which the virus keeps spreading, because people who fear being thrown out do not get tested. Teach the facts in Fig. 2 first; the conclusion then follows without needing to be insisted on.
- The spread practical is the best lesson in the whole strand. It needs only cups, water, one hidden cup of dilute sodium hydroxide, and an indicator such as phenolphthalein or universal indicator. Wear eye protection and brief the class beforehand that no real virus is involved - say it twice, because one pupil will always worry.
- The result that surprises them is not that it spreads. It is that they cannot tell who started it. Hold that thought and the whole of 17.7 follows from it.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**4.1  4.1 What is a Life Cycle?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) It is a cycle because it comes back to where it started: the adult produces eggs, the eggs become young, the young grow and change, and they become adults that produce eggs again. There is no real beginning or end - any stage can be a starting point, and each generation repeats what the last one did. A straight line would have a start and a finish, which is wrong. If the loop were broken at any point the species would end: if the adults died before laying eggs there would be no eggs; if the eggs did not hatch there would be no young; if the young did not survive to become adults there would be nothing to lay the next batch of eggs. Every stage is essential because every stage produces the next one.
- **Q2** (2 marks) Adult, eggs, young (larva or nymph), and growing and changing. Any order, one mark for each two named correctly.

**4.2  4.2 Stages of the Life Cycle of the Housefly: Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult**

- **Q3** (4 marks) A maggot has to moult because it is wrapped in an outer skin, the cuticle, which is fairly rigid and does not grow. As the body inside gets bigger the skin becomes too tight, so the larva splits it open and wriggles out in a newer, larger one underneath - and it does this twice. It is a COMPLETE metamorphosis because there are four clearly separate stages - egg, larva, pupa and adult - and the larva looks nothing like the adult: it has no wings, no legs, no compound eyes, and it lives and feeds in a completely different way. The change is not just growth, it is a rebuilding of the body, and most of that rebuilding happens out of sight inside the pupal case. In an incomplete metamorphosis the young resemble small adults and simply get bigger.
- **Q4** (3 marks) Adding up the times, a whole generation takes only about seven to twelve days: up to a day as an egg, three to five days as a larva, and three to six days as a pupa. So in roughly two weeks every egg has become an adult. And each female lays up to 150 eggs at a time, so one heap does not produce one fly - it produces dozens or hundreds, and every one of those new females immediately lays her own 150. The numbers multiply generation by generation, which is why the flies seem to appear all at once rather than gradually.

**4.3  4.3 Feeding Habits of the Housefly**

- **Q5** (4 marks) The fly has a sponging proboscis and no teeth or jaws, so it cannot bite and it cannot chew. That single fact drives everything that follows. Because it cannot take in solid food, it has to turn its food into a liquid first: it spits saliva onto whatever it has landed on, soaks it up, and sponges the liquid in. So to feed at all, the fly must make close contact with the surface of its food - and when that surface is faeces or rubbish, germs stick to the hairs on its legs and body and to its mouthparts. It then flies to the next meal, often our food, and does exactly the same thing there. The mouthparts are the reason the fly must touch filth and then touch food; the feeding method IS the transmission mechanism. A biting insect would inject germs straight into the blood - the fly simply walks them onto what we are about to eat.
- **Q6** (3 marks) Because it cannot bite or chew - it has no jaws and no teeth, only a sponging proboscis with a soft pad at the end. That pad can take up liquid but cannot bite pieces off solid food or grind them. So before it can feed on anything solid the fly has to dissolve it: it pours saliva over the food to soften and liquefy it, and then sponges up the liquid that results.

**4.4  4.4 How the Housefly Affects Human Health**

- **Q7** (4 marks) A fly lands on faeces, rubbish or a corpse, all of which teem with germs, and some of those germs stick to the hairs on its legs and body. It then flies off and lands on food - often cooked food left uncovered on a table - and walks over it, leaving the germs behind as it feeds and as it simply treads on it. A person then eats that food without reheating it and swallows the germs, which multiply in the gut and cause illness. Any one of these steps can be broken: cover the food so the fly cannot reach it; dispose of faeces in a latrine so the fly cannot reach them in the first place; screen the windows so flies cannot get in; or reheat food thoroughly before eating it.
- **Q8** (3 marks) The fly does not cause cholera and cannot give it to anyone on its own - it carries the bacterium that does. The disease is caused by the germ, Vibrio cholerae, which comes originally from the faeces of an infected person. The fly is only the vehicle: it picks the germ up on its legs and body and delivers it to food, without being infected itself. This is called mechanical transmission. The difference matters directly for control: if the fly were the cause, killing flies would end cholera. Because it is only one route among several, a household can be completely free of flies and still get cholera from contaminated water.

**4.5  4.5 Diseases Spread by the Housefly**

- **Q9** (3 marks) Typhoid. A vaccine works by preparing the immune system against one particular organism, and typhoid vaccine prepares it against the typhoid bacterium only. Cholera and dysentery are caused by different organisms, so the typhoid vaccine gives no protection against either of them. Those two are prevented in other ways - safe drinking water, washing hands with soap, using a latrine, and keeping food covered.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Any two symptoms: passing faeces containing blood and mucus; painful cramps in the abdomen; frequent, urgent passing of stool; fever. Any one prevention: dispose of faeces safely in a latrine so flies cannot reach them; wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before handling food; drink safe, clean water; keep cooked food covered.

**4.6  4.6 How to Reduce the Effects of Housefly Activities**

- **Q11** (4 marks) Spraying kills only the adult flies that are alive at that moment. The eggs, the larvae and the pupae are all still in the rubbish, sheltered inside the rotting material and, in the pupa's case, sealed inside a hard case that the spray cannot reach. Within a week those develop into adults and the population is back where it started - so spraying has to be repeated endlessly and only ever thins the flies temporarily. Removing breeding places - covered bins, latrines, clearing away rotting matter - means the next generation is never produced at all. The population falls and stays down. Killing the adults treats the symptom; denying them somewhere to breed treats the cause.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Screening the windows - and doors - with fine mesh or netting. The holes in the mesh are smaller than a housefly, so a fly cannot pass through them, but they are large enough for air to move through freely and for light to come in. So the house stays cool, lit and ventilated, but the flies are kept outside where they cannot reach the food.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) Houseflies breed on rotting organic matter that they are able to reach. Jar A, rotting fruit left open, produced many maggots, so rotting fruit is a suitable breeding material. Jar C, fresh cooked rice left open, produced none, so being reachable is not enough - the material has to be rotting. Jar D, dry soil left open, produced none, because there was no food in it for a larva to eat. And Jar B, the same rotting fruit but covered with net, produced none, showing that the flies must actually reach the material to lay eggs on it. Taken together: rotting matter, within reach of a fly.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Jar B contains exactly the same rotting fruit as Jar A, in the same kind of jar, left in the same place for the same five days - and it produced no maggots at all. The only difference between the two jars is the net over B that stopped flies from landing on the fruit. If rotting matter turned into maggots by itself, Jar B would have produced them just as Jar A did. Since it did not, the maggots cannot come from the fruit: they must come from eggs laid by flies that reached it. Jar B is the control that rules the prediction out.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. All four jars must be the same size and type, so that no jar gives the flies a bigger target or a different microclimate. They must all be left in the same place for the same five days, because a warmer or sunnier spot would speed up hatching and make that jar look like a better breeding site when it is only a warmer one. The same amount of material should be put in each jar. Whatever is used to cover Jar B must not shade it or change its temperature. Any of these differences would give a second explanation for the result, and the experiment would no longer show what it claims to show.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 72% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q5 is the best question in the paper. Pupils know the fly spreads disease; almost none can say WHY. The answer is the mouthparts: it cannot bite, so it must liquefy its food, so it must make contact with filth and then with our food. The feeding method is the transmission mechanism. Pupils who get this have connected 4.3 to 4.4.
- Q8 on 'the fly gives you cholera' is the companion to Q5. The distinction between cause and vehicle matters because it changes what control can achieve: a fly-free house can still have cholera from dirty water.
- Q11 on why spraying is less effective than removing breeding sites is the question that tests whether 4.6 has been understood or merely listed. Pupils like spraying because it is dramatic; the answer is that it leaves the next generation untouched.
- Q14 is the most valuable question in the practical. The belief that rotting matter turns into maggots is extremely common and extremely persistent, and Jar B is exactly the control that kills it. Do not let this one go by - ask the class to predict BEFORE the jars are opened, then hold them to it.
- The jar experiment in Fig. 7 costs nothing to run: four jars, some fruit, some net or muslin, and five days. Jar B must be covered with something flies cannot pass but air can. Run it in the last week before the topic so the results are ready to discuss.
- Note the timing arithmetic in Q4: egg plus larva plus pupa is about 7-12 days, so two weeks is one to two generations. Pupils who add the numbers get the answer; those who guess 'because there is a lot of rubbish' do not.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**2.1  2.1 What is a Cell? Introduction to Living Cells**

- **Q1** (3 marks) A single cell can only contract with the force of one cell. A tissue is many similar cells of the same kind working together, so their combined force is far greater and is enough to move a part of the body. One cell on its own cannot produce enough force to do that work.
- **Q2** (3 marks) It is an organism, not a tissue. The diagram shows that a tissue is a group of similar cells working together as part of a larger living thing. An amoeba is a single cell that carries out all of the life processes by itself, so it is a whole organism.

**2.2  2.2 Structure and Functions of the Animal Cell**

- **Q3** (3 marks) The cell membrane is the outer boundary: it holds the cell together and CONTROLS which substances enter and leave. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like material inside: it fills the cell and is where the chemical reactions of the cell take place.
- **Q4** (4 marks) The cell would run out of usable energy and would eventually die. Mitochondria carry out respiration, releasing the energy in food in a form the cell can use. Without that energy the cell cannot carry out the processes - growth, repair, moving substances - that keep it alive.

**2.3  2.3 Organelles of the Animal Cell and Their Functions**

- **Q5** (3 marks) 2 - mitochondrion: carries out respiration to release energy from food. 5 - vacuole: stores water, food and waste. (Also accept 5 - cytoplasm, which is where the cell's chemical reactions happen, depending on the reading of the figure.)
- **Q6** (3 marks) The nucleus contains the genetic material, which carries the instructions for making the cell's proteins and for everything the cell does. Because those instructions determine what the cell is and what it makes, the nucleus controls all the cell's activities.

**2.4  2.4 Structure and Functions of the Plant Cell**

- **Q7** (4 marks) A plant has no skeleton, so each of its cells must support itself. The cell wall is made of cellulose and is rigid, so it holds the cell firm and lets the plant stand upright. An animal has a skeleton to support its body, so its cells do not need a wall - and a wall would in fact stop them working, because animal cells such as muscle cells must be able to change shape.
- **Q8** (3 marks) The vacuole stores water and dissolved substances, and the water inside pushes the cytoplasm out against the wall so that the cell stays firm and the plant does not wilt. An animal cell does not rely on this for support because the animal has a skeleton, so its vacuoles are small and are used only for storage and for moving substances about inside the cell.

**2.5  2.5 Organelles of the Plant Cell and Their Functions**

- **Q9** (3 marks) 1 - cell wall.  4 - large central vacuole.  5 - chloroplast.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which traps light energy for photosynthesis. A plant in the dark has no light to trap, so it makes few chloroplasts because they would be of no use. This shows that the chloroplast is the organelle where the plant makes its own food using light.

**2.6  2.6 Differences and Similarities Between Plant and Animal Cells**

- **Q11** (3 marks) Any three: the plant cell has a cell wall, the animal cell does not. The plant cell has chloroplasts, the animal cell does not. The plant cell has one large central vacuole, the animal cell has small vacuoles. The plant cell has a regular, fixed rectangular shape, the animal cell has a rounded, irregular shape.
- **Q12** (4 marks) The two parts do different jobs. The cell membrane controls which substances enter and leave the cell, and every cell needs this. The plant also needs the rigid cell wall outside the membrane to hold the cell firm and support the plant, because a plant has no skeleton. The wall cannot replace the membrane because it is fully permeable - it lets everything through, so it cannot control what enters or leaves.
- **Q13** (3 marks) The reasoning is wrong because BOTH plant and animal cells have a nucleus, so a nucleus does not identify which kind of cell it is. The pupil should look for a cell wall, for chloroplasts, or for one large central vacuole, and at whether the cell has a fixed rectangular shape - these are found only in plant cells.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q14** (3 marks) Any two with a correction: the mirror or light source is not angled at the hole in the stage - turn it so that light is reflected up through the specimen. The objective lens is not lined up with the hole in the stage - rotate the nosepiece until it clicks into place. The slide is not sitting over the hole - move the slide across. The diaphragm is closed - open it.
- **Q15** (2 marks) A light microscope forms its image using light that passes THROUGH the specimen. If the specimen is too thick, light cannot get through it and it looks dark, so nothing can be seen.
- **Q16** (3 marks) Watch the objective from the SIDE while using the coarse knob to bring it down close to the slide. Then look down the eyepiece and use the coarse knob to focus by moving the lens UP, away from the slide. Watching from the side lets you see how close the lens is and stop before it touches the slide; focusing upwards means you can never push the lens into the glass.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 72% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 36% are Challenging. Use it to stretch pupils who already know the labels.
- Q7 and Q12 are the two hardest and they test the same idea from different directions: WHY a plant needs a wall. Pupils can name the parts but cannot say why the plant needs one and the animal does not. The answer they must reach is support - a plant has no skeleton, so every cell must hold itself up.
- Q12 has a second layer most pupils miss: the wall cannot do the membrane's job because it is fully permeable. If a pupil says 'the wall protects the cell and the membrane controls what goes in and out', they have both halves and deserve full marks.
- Q13 is the classic reasoning error - 'it has a nucleus so it must be a plant cell'. Both cells have a nucleus. Pupils should be taught to look for the wall, the chloroplasts or the single large vacuole instead.
- Q4, Q10 and Q14 all ask pupils to PREDICT or SUGGEST rather than recall. These are the words BECE uses and the ones pupils handle worst, because there is nothing to remember - the answer has to be reasoned from the diagram or from what the organelle does.
- The microscope in Fig. 7 is the cheapest practical in the syllabus and the one most likely to appear. If your school has even one working microscope, twenty minutes with an onion skin turns Q14 to Q16 into near-free marks. If it does not, the questions still work from the diagram alone.
- Q16 is worth teaching as a routine rather than an answer: focus DOWN while watching from the side, then focus UP while looking through the eyepiece. Say it as a rhyme and pupils remember it, and it saves the slides and the objective lenses.
