## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**1.1  1.1 States of Matter: Solids, Liquids and Gases**

- **Q1** (4 marks) In a solid the particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern and can only vibrate about fixed positions, so the solid keeps both its shape and its volume. In a gas the particles are far apart with large empty spaces between them, there are almost no forces holding them together, and they move freely and rapidly in all directions. A gas therefore spreads out to fill whatever container it is in - it takes the shape of the container and can be squeezed into a smaller volume, so it has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
- **Q2** (3 marks) The particles are exactly the same size in all three states - it is the same substance, only in a different state. What changes is the SPACING between the particles and how much they move, not the size of the particles themselves. In the gas there is a great deal of empty space between particles of unchanged size.
- **Q3** (2 marks) Arrangement: from a close, regular pattern (solid), to close together but irregular (liquid), to far apart and random (gas). Movement: from vibrating about fixed positions, to sliding past one another, to moving rapidly and freely in all directions.

**1.2  1.2 Properties and Differences Among Solids, Liquids and Gases**

- **Q4** (3 marks) In syringe R the substance is a gas, whose particles are far apart with large empty spaces between them, so pushing the plunger simply moves the particles closer together. In syringe P the substance is a solid, whose particles are already packed tightly together with almost no space between them, so there is nowhere for them to move to and the plunger will not go in.
- **Q5** (3 marks) The particles spread further apart so that they fill the whole of the larger space inside the syringe - the gas expands. This happens because the particles of a gas move rapidly and freely in all directions and are not held together, so they keep moving outwards until they are spread evenly through all the space available to them.

**1.3  1.3 Importance of Liquids to Human Life**

- **Q6** (4 marks) Any two, with the property and the reason: TRANSPORT OF BLOOD - liquids can flow, so blood can be pumped round the body carrying oxygen and dissolved food. COOKING - water stays liquid up to 100 degrees Celsius and transfers heat well, so food can be boiled in it. WASHING - a liquid can flow over a surface and dissolve the dirt, and then carry it away. WATERING CROPS - a liquid soaks into the soil and reaches the roots, which a solid could not do. COOLING MACHINES - water takes in a large amount of heat as it warms up, so it carries heat away from the machine.
- **Q7** (2 marks) A liquid can flow over and around the object being washed and can dissolve the dirt so that it is carried away. A solid cannot flow round the object and cannot dissolve the dirt off it.

**1.4  1.4 Importance of Solids to Human Life**

- **Q8** (4 marks) Any two with the property and the reason: IRON FOR A HOE - it is hard and can be sharpened to a cutting edge, and it does not bend when it is pushed into hard soil. BLOCKS FOR BUILDING - they are hard and strong under compression, so they carry the weight of the walls above them without crumbling. GRINDING STONES - they are hard and rough, so they wear the food down without themselves wearing away quickly. CHARCOAL FOR COOKING - it burns slowly and gives out a steady heat. POTS FOR COOKING - they withstand high temperatures without melting or catching fire.
- **Q9** (2 marks) Any one with a reason: A HOE - it must cut into hard soil without blunting or bending. GRINDING STONES - they must rub the food down without being worn away themselves. BUILDING BLOCKS - they must carry the weight above them without being crushed.

**1.5  1.5 The Periodic Table: Metals, Non-Metals and Noble Gases**

- **Q10** (3 marks) It would be a non-metal - specifically a noble gas. The diagram shows that Group 18, the far right-hand column, is the noble gas region, and noble gases are non-metals. Position from left to right decides whether an element is a metal, and Group 18 is at the far right.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Whether an element is a metal depends on its position from LEFT to RIGHT, not on how high up the table it sits. Lithium is in Group 1, the far left-hand column, which is inside the metal region. Fluorine is over on the right-hand side of the table, which is the non-metal region. Being near the top tells you nothing about whether it is a metal.

**1.6  1.6 Arrangement of Elements in the Periodic Table**

- **Q12** (2 marks) Magnesium: Period 3, Group 2. Chlorine: Period 3, Group 17.
- **Q13** (3 marks) Any two with a reason. They react in a similar way, because elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in the outer shell and it is the outer shell that controls how an element reacts. Both are soft metals that react vigorously with water, for the same reason. Both form compounds with the same ratio of atoms, e.g. with chlorine, because they form ions of the same charge.
- **Q14** (2 marks) A period is a horizontal ROW of elements; a group is a vertical COLUMN. The GROUP tells you more about how an element reacts, because elements in the same group react in similar ways.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q15** (1 mark) Filtration.
- **Q16** (2 marks) The sand is left on the filter paper - this is the residue. The salt water passes through - this is the filtrate.
- **Q17** (3 marks) Sand does not dissolve, so its particles stay clumped together in grains that are far too large to pass through the tiny pores in the filter paper. Salt DISSOLVES in the water, which means its particles are pulled apart and separated from one another, so each one is small enough to pass through the pores along with the water.
- **Q18** (2 marks) Place a cold surface or a condenser above the evaporating dish so that the water vapour cools, condenses back to a liquid, and runs down into a second container. The process would then be distillation.
- **Q19** (2 marks) Heat the dish gently, or use a water bath, or take the dish off the heat while there is still a little liquid left and let the last of the water evaporate in the heat of the dish. Any of these makes the water boil steadily instead of boiling violently, so bubbles do not burst and throw the solid crystals out of the dish.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- This paper is pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Integrated Science Paper 2. It is deliberately harder than a class test: 42% of the marks are Challenging and 76% are at Apply level or above. Use it for revision and for stretching your strongest pupils, not as a first teaching instrument.
- Only ONE mark in the whole paper is pure recall (Q15, naming filtration). Everything else asks pupils to explain, predict, justify or suggest - which is exactly the shape of the BECE compulsory question.
- Q2 is the key diagnostic. The belief that particles in a gas are LARGER is extremely common and survives right through to SHS. The diagram is drawn deliberately so the particles are the same size in all three boxes; if a pupil still says the gas particles are bigger, they have not grasped that state changes are about spacing and movement.
- Q11 targets the mirror-image error: pupils read the periodic table like a list and assume items near the top share properties. Properties run in columns, not rows. Drill this with lithium against fluorine.
- Q5 and Q19 both ask for a PREDICTION rather than a fact, which is where BECE lives. Pupils find 'predict' and 'suggest' far harder than 'state', because there is nothing to recall - they must reason from the diagram. Give them these two words explicitly before the examination.
- Q17 is the hardest practical question and the one most often answered wrongly. 'It dissolves' scores nothing; the mark is for dissolved particles being SEPARATED and therefore small enough to fit through the pores. Teach the word 'dissolved' as a statement about particle separation.
- The separation in Fig. 7 can be done for real in about twenty minutes using sand, salt, water, a funnel, filter paper and a tin dish. Doing it first turns Q15 to Q19 into near-free marks, and pupils who have seen the salt spit out of the dish answer Q19 from memory of the practical rather than by guessing.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**18.1  18.1 Careers in Science and How They Improve Human Life**

- **Q1** (4 marks) An industry is an organised process that takes a raw material and, through a series of steps, turns it into a finished product that people will buy. Ghana has traditionally shipped cocoa out as raw beans, so the roasting, grinding and pressing - and the branding, packaging and marketing that come after - have been done in Europe, and the value added at each of those stages has been earned there rather than here. A tonne of raw beans sells for a small fraction of what the chocolate made from that same tonne sells for. That is why grinding and processing cocoa in Ghana keeps more of the money at home. It is not that the beans are worth less; it is that nearly all the value is added after the farm, and whoever does the processing captures it.
- **Q2** (4 marks) Accept any raw material from the figure, marked on the quality of the processing chain and of the two difficulties. Model answer using cassava: the tubers are peeled, washed and grated; the pulp is pressed to squeeze out the milky liquid; that liquid is left to stand so the starch settles out, and the starch is then dried and bagged. Alternatively the grated pulp is fermented and roasted into gari. Difficulties: cassava spoils within two or three days of harvest, so the factory must be near the farms and must process immediately - it cannot build up a stockpile. And the supply is seasonal, so the plant may stand idle for part of the year. A third: cassava is also a food crop, so when the harvest fails the price rises and the factory is bidding against the food market for the same tubers.
- **Q3** (3 marks) Any three of: cocoa pods, crude oil, gold ore, bauxite, cassava, shea nuts, fish, timber, sugar cane.
- **Q4** (3 marks) A raw material is a natural substance, taken from the ground, the sea, the forest or the farm, which an industry processes into a product. Any two examples: cocoa pods, crude oil, gold ore, bauxite, cassava, shea nuts, fish, timber, sugar cane, palm fruit, cotton.

**18.2  18.2 Ghanaian Scientists and Their Contributions**

- **Q5** (4 marks) Accept any accurate pair, marked on the accuracy of the work and on the link to a real need. Model answer: Marian Ewurama Addy worked on the biochemistry of herbal medicine, testing plant remedies to find out which of them contain active compounds and what those compounds do. This mattered in Ghana because herbal medicine is what most people actually use, yet almost none of it had been tested; her work began the job of separating the remedies that work from those that do not, and of making them safe and properly dosed. Isaac Newton worked on motion, gravity and light, and showed that the same law governs a falling stone and the orbit of the moon. This mattered because it replaced a collection of separate rules with one law you could calculate with, which is what made engineering and navigation possible. The two are doing the same thing: replacing what people assumed with what could be shown.
- **Q6** (3 marks) Francis Allotey - mathematical physics. Marian Ewurama Addy - biochemistry. Ibok Oduro - food science and post-harvest technology. (Accept any two with the correct field.)
- **Q7** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Their work is the evidence for what we are taught: knowing who established something, and how they showed it, is what separates a fact from an opinion. The way they worked - measuring carefully, repeating, questioning what everyone believed - is the method pupils are being taught, and a real example shows the method better than a definition can. Several of them, notably Addy and Oduro, chose problems that mattered where they lived, which shows that science is not only done in rich countries on abstract questions.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Accept any one, accurately stated. Francis Allotey: work on soft X-ray spectroscopy, and the Allotey Formalism named after him; the first Ghanaian professor of mathematics. Marian Ewurama Addy: research on the biochemistry of herbal medicines; the first Ghanaian woman to become a full professor of natural science. Ibok Oduro: food science and post-harvest technology, including fortified sweet potato to address vitamin A deficiency. From the international list: Newton - laws of motion and universal gravitation; Darwin - evolution by natural selection; Curie - radioactivity, discovered radium and polonium; Pasteur - germ theory, pasteurisation, vaccines.

**18.4  18.4 Science, Technology and Innovation in Ghana**

- **Q9** (4 marks) She needs biology, with some chemistry for soils and fertilisers. In the job she would visit farms to work out why a crop is failing - which means looking closely, taking samples and testing them rather than guessing - and she would advise farmers which variety to plant and when, which depends on records of what has done well in previous seasons. The skills in Fig. 3 matter because they ARE the job. Observing carefully, and writing down what she actually saw rather than what she expected, is the difference between a correct diagnosis and a wasted season for the farmer. Measuring, and repeating - soil samples from several points across a field rather than one - is what stops a wrong recommendation. Keeping records is what lets her say next year whether the advice worked. Working safely applies to handling fertilisers and agrochemicals. An officer who cannot do these things is not an officer, however much biology she knows.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Any two, each described. An electrical engineer designs and maintains power systems and wiring. A civil engineer designs roads, bridges and buildings and checks that they will carry their loads. An electrician installs and repairs wiring and equipment. A geologist searches for minerals and advises on how to extract them. A surveyor measures land and marks boundaries. A meteorologist measures the weather and forecasts it. A pilot flies aircraft and must understand the forces acting on them.
- **Q11** (3 marks) Because a result that was not written down is a result that was never taken. It cannot be checked, repeated, compared with last month, or used to show a client or a court what was actually done. In a laboratory, a workshop and on a farm, the record is what makes the work trustworthy, and it is what lets a mistake be traced back to its cause. An employer cannot watch everything a worker does, so the record is also the evidence that the work was done properly at all.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q12** (4 marks) Cassava gives the most, at 25 g of starch from every 100 g of crop - about a quarter of its mass. Sweet potato gives the least, at 11 g, so cassava yields more than twice as much. A factory cares because this is the number that decides its costs: a tonne of cassava gives 250 kg of starch, but a tonne of sweet potato gives only 110 kg, so the cassava is worth more than twice as much per tonne even if both cost the same to buy. That determines the price the factory can afford to pay farmers, and therefore which crop the farmers around it should grow - and whether the factory can compete at all. Fairness matters because the figure is worthless if the comparison was not fair. If one sample was squeezed harder, left to settle for longer, or started with more water, that alone could account for the whole difference. Same mass, same water, same settling time, repeated and averaged - that is not fussiness, it is what makes the number mean anything.
- **Q13** (3 marks) Repeating and averaging protects against the fact that how hard you squeeze the cloth changes the answer more than the crop does, and against losing a little sediment when the water is poured off. A single trial may be high or low for a reason that has nothing to do with which crop was used. What must be kept the same: the same mass of each crop (100 g), the same volume of water for sieving, the same settling time, and the same way of pouring the water off. If any of those differed, the experiment would be measuring the method rather than the crop.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Starch grains do not dissolve in water and are denser than it, so given time they sink under gravity and collect at the bottom as a layer of sediment, leaving clear water above that can be poured off. If the mixture were shaken instead, the starch would be stirred back up and dispersed through the water; it would stay in suspension rather than settling, and when the water was poured off most of the starch would go with it. The yield would then appear far lower than it really is. Settling needs the mixture to be left completely still.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Dry the starch completely - in an oven or in the sun - and weigh it again, so the mass is dry starch rather than starch with water still in it; wet starch weighs more and the yield is overstated. Wash the sediment: stir it up in clean water, let it settle again and pour off, which removes fibre and other material carried over and leaves purer starch. Sieve through a finer cloth and do it twice, so less starch is lost in the pulp that is discarded. Weigh each crop after peeling rather than before, since the amount of peel differs between crops and would otherwise distort the comparison.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the question that makes 18.1 worth teaching. Ghana sells cocoa beans and buys back chocolate. The reason is not that the beans are worth less - it is that almost all the value is added after the farm, and whoever does the processing captures it. Pupils grasp this immediately, and it is the whole argument for industrialisation in one example.
- Q2 is deliberately open: it asks the pupil to choose a raw material from their own region. Mark it on the quality of the processing chain and of the two difficulties, not on which crop they picked. The best answers notice that perishability and seasonality are problems for any food-crop factory.
- Q5 and Q8 cover 18.2 and 18.3, which dg_survey flagged as having no drawable content. They are recall of names and contributions, so they are pitched at Understand and Analyse rather than pretending to be application. Q5 is the only way to make the strand worth anything: it asks why the work MATTERED, not just what it was.
- Note on the source material: the curriculum's list includes a 'Paul Ratnei' which I could not trace in any source. No question here tests that name, and it is worth flagging to the curriculum team.
- The starch practical works well with cassava, yam, plantain, cocoyam and sweet potato, all cheap and available. You need graters, cloth for sieving, and a balance. Cassava is genuinely dramatic - it gives more than twice the sweet potato - which makes the point about industrial raw-material choice better than any graph.
- Graters are the real hazard. Brief the class to grate downwards with fingers clear, and consider grating the samples yourself as a demonstration if the group is large.
- If you have no balance accurate to a gram, drying and weighing is still worth doing roughly - the ranking of the crops is robust enough to survive a coarse measurement.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**14.9  14.9 Simple Machines and Their Types**

- **Q1** (4 marks) The work is identical: lifting straight up is 500 N x 1 m = 500 J, and pushing up the slope is 125 N x 4 m = 500 J. What the slope changes is not the amount of work but the SIZE OF THE FORCE you must supply at any one moment. Lifting straight up demands a single pull of 500 N, which is beyond one person. The slope lets the same job be done with a pull of only 125 N - a force one person can manage - but you have to keep pushing over 4 m instead of 1 m. So 'easier' means 'with a smaller effort', not 'with less work'. The machine changes the force and charges you in distance; it cannot reduce the total work.
- **Q2** (3 marks) A machine is a device that makes work easier by changing the size or the direction of a force. No machine can give out more work than is put into it - it cannot produce more energy than it receives, and some of what goes in is always lost as heat.

**14.10  14.10 Types and Functions of Levers**

- **Q3** (4 marks) (a) A lever. It makes the force bigger: a small pull on the handle produces a large pull on the cap. (b) A pulley. It changes the direction: you pull down on the rope and the flag travels up. The effort is about the same size as the load, which is the price of that convenience. (c) A wedge. It makes the force bigger and turns it sideways: a downward blow becomes a large splitting force pushing the wood apart. (d) An inclined plane. It makes the force smaller for the same job: pushing the load up the ramp needs far less force than lifting it straight onto the truck, but over a longer distance.
- **Q4** (3 marks) Any three of: lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, screw, wedge, gears, hydraulic press.
- **Q5** (3 marks) A spanner is a lever, and the turning effect it produces depends on both the force you apply and how far from the pivot - the nut - it acts. With a long spanner, the same push from your hand acts at a greater distance from the nut, so it gives a bigger turning effect and the nut gives way. With a short spanner you would have to push much harder to get the same turning effect, and beyond a point you simply cannot.
- **Q6** (3 marks) If you could unwrap the thread of a screw and lay it out flat, it would be one long sloping line - an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder. Driving the screw in is like pushing a load up that slope: the further you push along the slope for each centimetre gained, the less force you need. Closely spaced threads mean many turns for every centimetre the screw advances, so the slope is shallower and the same push gives a larger inward force. The cost is that you must turn the screw many more times to drive it the same depth.

**14.11  14.11 Work Input, Work Output and Efficiency**

- **Q7** (4 marks) The velocity ratio is fixed by the geometry of the machine - how much further the effort travels than the load does - and nothing can alter it. The mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load actually lifted to the effort actually needed. In a perfect machine the two would be equal and the efficiency would be 100%. But in a real machine part of your effort goes into overcoming friction between the moving parts, and part into lifting the machine's own moving parts, neither of which benefits the load. So you have to pull harder than the geometry alone demands, the mechanical advantage comes out below the velocity ratio, and the difference is work converted into heat. That gap is precisely what efficiency measures, as M.A. over V.R.
- **Q8** (4 marks) Mechanical advantage = load / effort = 200 N / 50 N = 4. Velocity ratio = 5. Efficiency = M.A. / V.R. x 100% = 4 / 5 x 100% = 80%. So 80% of the work put in comes out as useful work on the load. The missing 20% has been converted into heat by friction between the moving parts of the machine, and into raising the machine's own moving parts. The energy has not been destroyed - it has simply ended up somewhere useless, warming the machine and the air around it. That is why no machine can ever reach 100% efficiency.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Oil or grease the axle so the sheave turns more freely, which cuts the friction that turns useful work into heat. Fit ball bearings at the axle for the same reason. Use lighter, more flexible rope, so less of the effort is spent lifting and bending the rope itself rather than the load. Lift a heavier load: the effort wasted on friction and on the moving parts stays roughly the same, so as a fraction of a bigger useful output it shrinks, and the efficiency rises.
- **Q10** (3 marks) The ratio of the distance moved by the effort to the distance moved by the load, measured over the same time. It says how much further your hand has to travel than the load does. Unlike the mechanical advantage it is fixed by the shape and arrangement of the machine and is not affected by friction.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q11** (4 marks) The effort needed depends entirely on how the pivot divides the lever. In set-up 1 the effort arm is 80 cm and the load arm 20 cm - four times as long - and the 10 N load needs only 2.6 N, so the lever is multiplying the effort about fourfold. In set-up 2 the two arms are equal at 50 cm each; there is no multiplication at all and the effort is 10.4 N, essentially the weight of the load plus a little extra for friction. In set-up 3 the arms are reversed, 20 cm and 80 cm, and the effort jumps to 42 N - now the lever works against you and you push roughly four times harder than the load weighs. So the longer the effort arm is compared with the load arm, the less effort is needed, and the ratio of the two arms is the velocity ratio.
- **Q12** (4 marks) Velocity ratio = effort arm / load arm = 80 cm / 20 cm = 4.0. Mechanical advantage = load / effort = 10 N / 2.6 N = 3.8 (3.85 to 3 s.f.). Efficiency = M.A. / V.R. x 100% = 3.8 / 4.0 x 100% = 95%. An efficiency of about 95% says that nearly all the work put in comes out as useful work lifting the load, and only about 5% is lost. The loss is friction where the lever turns on the pivot, and it is small because a lever has only one rubbing surface. That is why the lever is among the most efficient of the simple machines. Notice too that the efficiency stays near 95% in all three set-ups - the friction is much the same whatever the geometry, so changing the pivot position changes the effort needed but not how much is wasted.
- **Q13** (4 marks) He should place the pivot as close to the stone as he can get it, leaving the longest possible effort arm and the shortest possible load arm. That gives the largest velocity ratio, so the force-multiplying effect is at its greatest and the effort needed is at its smallest. The disadvantage is distance: because the work is the same either way, gaining force costs movement, so he must now push his end of the lever through a much greater distance to raise the stone by a little. He also needs a longer, stiffer lever, strong enough not to bend, and he needs room to swing it.
- **Q14** (2 marks) The distance from the pivot to the point where the effort is applied.
- **Q15** (2 marks) The force that the machine has to overcome - here, the weight of the object being lifted, which is the 10 N weight hanging from the lever.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 74% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the question the whole strand rests on, and it is worth doing slowly at the board. Pupils come in believing a machine 'saves work'. It does not: 500 J either way. What it does is let you use a smaller force, and it charges you for that in distance. Get this right and mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency all follow from it; get it wrong and the rest of 14.11 is arithmetic without meaning.
- Q7 and Q8 are a pair. Q7 asks why M.A. is always below V.R.; Q8 makes them calculate it. The sentence to listen for is 'friction takes its cut' - the difference between the two ratios is work turned into heat, not work that vanished.
- Q6 on the screw as a spiral inclined plane is the one pupils enjoy, and it is worth drawing the unwrapped thread on the board. It also explains something they have all noticed: fine threads are easier to drive but take far longer to go in.
- Q12 is the calculation question, and the interesting part is the last sentence. The efficiency stays near 95% across all three set-ups because the friction at the pivot does not care where the pivot is. Pupils expect efficiency to vary with the geometry; it does not, and saying why is worth more than the arithmetic.
- For the lever experiment you need a metre rule or a wooden lath, a triangular or round pivot, a 10 N weight and a spring balance. Drill or notch the rule at 20, 50 and 80 cm so the pivot cannot roll. The awkward measurement is the effort in set-up 3 - 42 N will overload a 10 N balance, so use a 50 N balance for that one, or predict the value first and let pupils discover the problem themselves.
- If balances are short, run the three set-ups as a demonstration with pupils recording the readings, then let groups repeat just one set-up each.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**8.1  8.1 What is the Solar System?**

- **Q1** (4 marks) The sun is at the centre. The sun's gravity pulls on every planet, and that inward pull is what holds each planet in its orbit. Without it, a planet would carry on in a straight line and travel off into space. Each planet is moving forwards, and the sun's pull bends that forward motion into a curve, so the planet goes round the sun instead of either falling into it or flying away.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any one with an explanation. The inner four are small and rocky while the outer four are much bigger - the diagram shows the outer orbits are far apart and the planets drawn on them are larger. Or: the outer planets take far longer to go once round the sun, because their orbits are much larger so they have a much greater distance to travel. Or: the inner planets are hot and the outer ones cold, because the inner four are close to the sun.

**8.2  8.2 The Galaxy and the Milky Way**

- **Q3** (3 marks) The Milky Way is a galaxy - an enormous collection of many millions of stars held together by gravity. Our sun is ONE of those stars, and it sits out in one of the spiral arms, a long way from the centre of the galaxy, not at the centre of it.
- **Q4** (3 marks) They are completely different sizes of thing. The solar system is ONE star, the sun, together with the planets, moons and other bodies going round it. The Milky Way is a galaxy containing many millions of stars, and the sun is only one of them. So the solar system sits inside the Milky Way as a tiny part of it - they cannot be the same thing.

**8.3  8.3 The Inner Planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars**

- **Q5** (3 marks) Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars. Mercury is nearest the sun.
- **Q6** (4 marks) A year is the time a planet takes to travel once round the sun. Mercury's orbit is much smaller than the earth's because Mercury is much closer to the sun, so it has a far shorter distance to cover. Mercury also travels faster along its orbit than the earth does. Smaller distance and greater speed both mean one complete journey round the sun takes far less time - 88 earth days against the earth's 365.

**8.4  8.4 Properties of the Inner Planets**

- **Q7** (4 marks) The year gets longer as you move outwards: 88 earth days on Mercury, 225 on Venus, 365 on Earth, 687 on Mars. The reason is that the further a planet is from the sun, the larger its orbit, so it has a greater distance to travel to get once round. The further planets also move more slowly along their orbits, so the journey takes longer still.
- **Q8** (3 marks) A day and a year are two completely separate movements, and their lengths do not have to be related. A day is the time the planet takes to spin once on its own axis; a year is the time it takes to travel once round the sun. Venus spins on its axis extremely slowly - more slowly than it goes round the sun - so one spin takes 243 earth days while one orbit takes only 225.

**8.5  8.5 Movement of Mercury and Venus Around the Sun**

- **Q9** (4 marks) Both orbits lie INSIDE the orbit of the earth, so Mercury and Venus are always in roughly the same direction from the earth as the sun is. We can therefore only ever see them near the sun in the sky - low in the west just after sunset, or low in the east just before sunrise. At midnight the sun, and with it the direction these planets lie in, is on the far side of the earth, so they cannot be seen then.
- **Q10** (3 marks) Mercury takes less time. The diagram shows Mercury's orbit is the smaller of the two, so Mercury is closer to the sun and has a shorter distance to travel to complete one orbit. A smaller orbit means a shorter journey, and so a shorter year.

**8.6  8.6 Elliptical Paths of the Planets**

- **Q11** (3 marks) An ellipse is an oval shape - like a circle that has been stretched out in one direction. In the orbit shown the sun is not at the centre of the ellipse but at one FOCUS, which is one of the two points set inwards from the ends of the oval.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Because the orbit is an ellipse and not a circle, and the sun sits at one focus rather than at the centre. That means one end of the orbit is nearer the sun than the other. The diagram shows this: the distance marked NEAREST is shorter than the distance marked FURTHEST, so the earth's distance from the sun changes as it goes round.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) Push a stick upright into flat, open ground. Mark the position of the tip of its shadow on the ground every hour, and note the time beside each mark. Through the day the shadow swings round and changes length - long in the morning, shortest at midday, long again in the evening, pointing the other way by late afternoon. The sun is not moving round the earth, so the only way the shadow can swing round like that is if the earth itself is turning. The pattern of marks is the record of the earth's rotation.
- **Q14** (3 marks) At midday the sun is higher in the sky than at any other time of the day - it is more nearly overhead. The higher the sun is, the more steeply its rays come down, and the more steeply they come down the shorter the shadow they cast. So the shortest shadow marks the moment the sun is highest.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any one with a remedy. The ground may not be level, which tilts the stick and falsely changes the shadow length - check with a spirit level or choose the flattest ground you can find. The tip of the shadow is fuzzy and hard to mark exactly - mark the middle of the fuzzy edge, and have the same person judge it every time. The stick may lean over during the day - check it stays upright. Cloud may hide the sun for part of the day - choose a clear day, or repeat on another day and compare.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 70% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q1 is the one pupils answer with 'gravity' and nothing else, and they score one of four. To get the rest they must say what the pull DOES: it bends the planet's forward motion into a curve, so the planet neither falls into the sun nor flies off in a straight line. Teach it as 'forwards plus inwards equals around'.
- Q4 on the Milky Way against the solar system is the confusion I meet most. Pupils use the two words interchangeably. The scale contrast is the cure: the solar system has one star, the galaxy has millions, and the sun is one of them.
- Q8 - a day on Venus longer than its year - is the best 'explain how this can be true' question in the paper, because the answer is that the two movements are independent. Pupils assume a year must be longer than a day and are stuck. Venus spins so slowly that it breaks the assumption.
- Q9, on why Mercury and Venus are never seen at midnight, is genuinely hard and needs the diagram. Their orbits are inside ours, so their direction from us is always close to the sun's direction. Very few pupils reach this without seeing Fig. 5.
- The shadow-stick practical in Fig. 7 is the best astronomy practical available to a school with no equipment at all - a stick, some chalk and a level playground. Run it across a whole school day with hourly marks and Q13 to Q15 become straightforward. It also gives pupils a real record of rotation rather than a diagram they have to believe.
- Note on Q11: 'oval' is worth one mark, but the point pupils miss is the FOCUS - the sun is off-centre, which is exactly why the distance changes in Q12. The two questions are a pair; teach them together.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**20.1  20.1 Landforms in Ghana: Plateau, Plain, Mountain and Valley**

- **Q1** (4 marks) The biotic part is everything that is alive - plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. The abiotic part is the non-living surroundings: sunlight, water, soil, air, temperature, minerals. They are not separate boxes, because the living part depends on the non-living part absolutely. The plants need sunlight, water, carbon dioxide and minerals from the soil before they can make any food at all; the animals then depend on the plants; the decomposers depend on the dead remains; and when they rot it, the nutrients go back into the soil for the plants again. So change an abiotic factor and the whole living system moves. Take away the water and the plants stop growing, the animals that eat them starve or move away, and the decomposers run out of material. That is why an environment is described as a SYSTEM rather than a place - and why a change in something as ordinary as rainfall can empty a landscape of its animals.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Biotic, any three: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria. Abiotic, any three: sunlight, water, soil, air, temperature, minerals, rainfall.
- **Q3** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. The floodplain plants that depended on the annual flood for water and for the silt it deposited would die back or be replaced by species that can manage without it; the plant community changes, and with it the animals that fed on those plants. Fish that used the flooded margins as a nursery, or that spawned upstream, would lose those breeding grounds, so the fish population falls - and with it the fishermen and the birds that ate them. Animals that moved onto the plain in the dry season would lose the grazing. And the soil would no longer be refreshed with silt each year, so it becomes steadily less fertile.

**20.2  20.2 Plants and Animals Found in Different Landforms**

- **Q4** (4 marks) Because the gold is a small part of what gets disturbed. Getting at it means stripping the vegetation and the topsoil off the bank and washing enormous quantities of soil and gravel, so the soil structure, the seed bank and the soil life that took centuries to build are destroyed and the land is left unable to grow anything. All that disturbed soil ends up in the river, silting it, blocking the light and smothering the gravel beds where fish spawn - so the fish disappear and the fishermen downstream lose their living. And the mercury and cyanide used to separate the gold go into the water as well. Mercury does not wash away; it accumulates up the food chain, so it ends up concentrated in the fish that people eat. So the real cost is not the gold that was taken. It is a river that no longer supports fish, a bank that no longer supports crops, and a water supply that is no longer safe - and the people who pay are not the people who took the gold.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Any three: deforestation, bush burning, overfishing, bad farming (monocropping, ploughing down the slope, burning crop residue), mining or galamsey, pollution, overgrazing, draining wetlands.

**20.3  20.3 How Animals Adapt to Different Landforms**

- **Q6** (4 marks) Once the topsoil washes or blows away, the land grows less food, because the topsoil is where the nutrients and the organic matter are. A family getting a smaller harvest from a plot has to find the missing food somewhere, and the usual answer is to clear another piece of bush and plant more land. But the new plot has the same soil and the same slope, so it erodes in turn, and in a few years it too is exhausted - so the family clears more again. Each step is forced by the one before: less soil, less food, more land cleared, less soil. The circle tightens because the remedy the family can afford - more land - is the very thing that makes the problem worse, and it keeps going until there is no more land left to clear.
- **Q7** (3 marks) The trees were intercepting the rain on their leaves and slowing it, so it reached the ground gently; their roots were holding the soil together and opening channels in it, so much of the water soaked in instead of running off. Without them, the rain hits bare ground at full force, the surface seals and compacts, and the water runs straight off carrying soil with it. So instead of arriving gradually over days, the same rain arrives in the valley within hours - a flood. And the soil it carries fills the river bed and the drains, so the channel holds less and the next flood is worse still.
- **Q8** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. Loss of soil through erosion. Loss of biodiversity - species dying out. Rivers and streams drying up or silting. Flooding, because water runs off faster than it used to. Lower crop yields. Loss of fish stocks. Water that is no longer safe to drink.

**20.4  20.4 How Plants Survive in Different Landforms**

- **Q9** (4 marks) Any two, each explained by mechanism. Plant hedges, grass strips or trees along the contour - across the slope rather than down it - so that the stems slow the water running downhill and the roots bind the soil particles together; the water then has time to soak in instead of carrying the soil away. Plough and plant on the contour, making ridges across the slope, so each ridge acts as a small dam that catches the water and any soil it is carrying. Keep crop residue on the surface as a mulch instead of burning it, so that raindrops hit the residue rather than bare soil and the surface does not seal. Plant trees on the steepest land and farm only the gentler ground. Terrace the slope, so that each level is flat and the water cannot accelerate downhill.
- **Q10** (3 marks) The strip's roots bind the bank so that it does not collapse into the water, and its stems slow the water running off the field so that soil is filtered out and dropped before it reaches the river, rather than silting it. The vegetation also shades the water, keeping it cooler, and its leaves and insects feed the fish. For the farmer it holds his soil on his own land rather than washing it into the river, so his field stays fertile; it keeps the river channel clear, so it floods his land less often; and it gives him a crop of poles, fodder or fruit into the bargain.

**20.5  20.5 Associations Among Plants and Animals**

- **Q11** (4 marks) The capital is the stock itself - the forest, the breeding fish, the soil. The interest is what that stock produces each year without being reduced: the timber the forest puts on in a year, the surplus of young fish, the humus the soil rebuilds. Using the environment sustainably means taking the interest and leaving the capital intact, so that next year there is the same stock producing the same surplus, and the year after that, indefinitely. Using it unsustainably means eating into the capital: felling more trees than grow back, netting the young fish before they have spawned, cropping the soil year after year without putting anything back. That yields more today and nothing tomorrow. Sustainable does not mean doing without - it means arranging things so that the taking can go on.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Using the environment to meet our needs now without reducing its ability to meet the needs of people in future - in short, taking no more than is replaced. Any one example: cutting only mature trees and planting a seedling for each one felled. Or fishing with a net whose mesh lets the young fish through, so that the stock can breed. Or leaving a field fallow so that the soil recovers between crops.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (3 marks) The bare tray lost 31 g of soil and the grassy tray only 4 g - less than a seventh - and the grassy tray soaked up 320 ml of water against 110 ml, nearly three times as much. The grass does three things. Its leaves intercept the water so that it does not strike the soil at full force and knock the particles about. Its roots bind the particles together so they cannot easily be lifted and carried. And its stems slow the water flowing down the slope, giving it time to soak in instead of running off. Run-off is what carries soil away, so slowing the water does both jobs at once: more water in the soil and less soil in the run-off. And the first soil to go is the topsoil, the layer with the nutrients in it - which is why erosion does far more damage than the mass of soil lost suggests.
- **Q14** (3 marks) Any three, each explained. The same soil, at the same depth and firmed down the same amount in both trays - otherwise one tray simply has more soil available to lose. Both trays at the same angle of tilt, so that gravity pulls the water down both at the same rate. The same volume of water, poured from the same height at the same rate, so that the force of the water is the same. The same size and shape of tray. And the soil collected must be dried before it is weighed, or the water clinging to it will be weighed as if it were soil.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any one, tested and explained. Test steeper slopes: tip both trays at a greater angle, and expect both to lose more soil, because water moves faster down a steeper slope and carries more - which is why contour planting matters most on steep land. Test bare soil against soil covered with a mulch of dried grass rather than living plants: expect the mulch to give much of the protection, since it is the covering of the surface that breaks the force of the drops - which would show that leaving crop residue on the field is worth doing even before any roots have grown. Test a third tray with grass only a week old against the established one, to find out how quickly the protection develops.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 38% are Challenging.
- Q4 on galamsey is the paper's most important question, and in much of Ghana it is not an abstraction. The point to draw out is that the gold is a small part of what gets disturbed: the soil, the river and the mercury are the real cost, and the people who pay are downstream of the people who profited.
- Q6 on the erosion circle is the one that pupils find genuinely uncomfortable, and worth spending time on. Poor farmers clear more bush not because they are careless but because they have no alternative - and clearing more bush is what makes the problem worse. It is a circle, and the honest answer is that the family cannot break it alone.
- Q11 on capital and interest is the clearest way I know to teach sustainability. Take the interest, leave the capital. It also settles the argument that sustainability means doing without: it does not, it means arranging the taking so it can continue.
- The erosion practical needs two trays or wooden boxes with a lip at the lower end, the same soil in both, a measuring cylinder, and something to catch the run-off. Grass seed needs sowing two or three weeks beforehand, so plan ahead - or use a square of turf lifted intact, which works just as well and needs no notice.
- The soil in the run-off must be dried before weighing, or you weigh water with it. Filtering through filter paper and leaving it overnight, or drying it in an oven if you have one, both work.
- If you cannot get turf or seed, the mulch variant in Q15 is easier: scatter dried grass over the bare tray. It still shows most of the effect, because most of the protection comes from covering the surface.

## ANSWER KEY AND MARKING SCHEME

**16.1  16.1 Types of Waste in the Environment**

- **Q1** (4 marks) Sorting by where the waste was found tells you who dropped it, but nothing about what to do with it. Sorting by material tells you what the substance actually is, and therefore what can be done with it: whether it rots, whether it can be melted and remade, whether it is dangerous to touch. A hospital produces both used needles and food scraps from its kitchen. The needles must go into a puncture-proof sharps box and be incinerated; the food scraps can simply be composted. If you sorted them together as 'hospital waste' you would either have to treat both as infectious, which is expensive, or treat both as ordinary, which is dangerous. The material, not the address, decides the disposal route.
- **Q2** (3 marks) Any three of: household, market, school or office, farm, hospital, industry or workshop, electronic, the street.
- **Q3** (3 marks) (a) From a farm; made of plastic, with chemical residue still inside. (b) From a household or dropped in the street; made of polythene film, a plastic. (c) From a market or a kitchen; made of plant material, so it is organic and will rot.

**16.2  16.2 Good Waste Management Practices**

- **Q4** (4 marks) The rubbish contains faeces - from nappies, from a latrine that has overflowed, from animals. Flies breed in it and then land on food laid out in the house or the market, carrying the bacteria on their feet and mouthparts and depositing them when they feed. The child eats the food and the bacteria reach the gut. Or rain washes the waste into a stream or an open well that the family draws water from, and the child drinks it. Either way the waste never touches the child: the fly, or the water, carries it. That is why the remedy is not to keep children away from the dump - it is to separate faeces from flies and from water in the first place, which means a proper latrine and proper collection.
- **Q5** (3 marks) Any three, each stated. Cholera and dysentery, spread by flies and by contaminated water. Malaria, because discarded tins and sachets hold water in which mosquitoes breed. Breathing trouble and coughs from the fumes of burning plastic. Blocked drains, which flood the street and leave standing water. Poisoning of soil and water by chemicals and batteries.
- **Q6** (3 marks) Any two, each explained. Clear the drains and keep them clear, so that water can run away instead of ponding and breeding mosquitoes. Reduce the plastic at source - discourage or ban single-use polythene bags and promote reusable ones - so that the drains do not choke again within a month. Provide enough bins and a reliable collection, so that plastic has somewhere to go other than the gutter. Fit gratings over drain entrances to catch bags before they get in.

**16.3  16.3 The Science Behind Waste Management**

- **Q7** (4 marks) Because recycling is not free. Collecting the material, transporting it, sorting it, washing it and then reprocessing it all take energy, and the reprocessing produces waste of its own: paper fibres get shorter every time they are pulped, and plastic degrades every time it is melted. Reducing means the material was never made into a throwaway product in the first place, so none of that is spent - no collection, no transport, no reprocessing, no losses. A bottle refilled a hundred times costs a fraction of a hundred bottles recycled a hundred times. That is why the hierarchy runs reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose: the higher up the list, the less energy is spent and the less waste is created. Recycling is what you do with material you failed to avoid making.
- **Q8** (3 marks) (a) REDUCE - you avoid taking a new bag, so less waste is created in the first place. (b) RECYCLE - the glass is broken down and reprocessed into something new, which costs energy. (c) REUSE - the tyre is used again just as it is, with no reprocessing at all.
- **Q9** (3 marks) Recycling is collecting a waste material, reprocessing it, and making it into a new product, so that the material is used again instead of being thrown away. Any two commonly recycled materials: paper and card, glass, metals such as aluminium cans and scrap iron, and some plastics.

**16.4  16.4 Community Waste Management Projects**

- **Q10** (4 marks) A food scrap will rot. It is organic and harmless, and left to decompose it becomes compost that can be dug into the garden. A used needle can carry HIV or hepatitis B in the trace of blood inside the barrel, and it delivers that blood straight through the skin into the bloodstream of anyone who steps on it or picks it up. So the two are at opposite ends of the danger scale and cannot go into the same bin. The food scrap goes into a compost pit or an organic waste bin and ends up as manure. The needle goes straight into a puncture-proof sharps box - never into an ordinary bin, where it will injure whoever empties it - and the sealed box is then incinerated or buried deep. The general rule is that the more dangerous the waste, the further it must be kept from people, water and food.
- **Q11** (3 marks) An empty container still holds a film of the concentrate, visible or not, and rinsing it once leaves more than enough chemical behind to poison anyone who drinks from it. These containers are also attractive to children and look exactly like water containers, which is how accidental poisoning usually happens. What should be done: triple-rinse it, pouring the rinse water into the spray tank so it is used rather than spilled; then puncture or crush it so that nobody can ever reuse it; and return it to the supplier or a designated collection point. It must never be burnt, because the fumes are toxic, and never thrown into a river or the bush.
- **Q12** (3 marks) Electronic waste contains heavy metals and other hazardous substances - lead in solder and screens, mercury in some switches and lamps, cadmium in batteries. When the item is dumped these leak into the soil and the water; if it is burnt they give off toxic fumes. Any two items: mobile phones, batteries, chargers and cables, computers, televisions, radios, burnt-out appliances.

**PRACTICAL TASK**

- **Q13** (4 marks) The audit shows that more than half the waste - 4.2 kg out of 8.3 kg, or 51% - is organic material that rots, and so could be composted rather than burnt or dumped. A further 44% is paper, plastic and glass that could be recycled. Only a small fraction cannot be diverted at all. A quarter of everything is plastic, and most of that is sachet water bags, which points at one specific habit rather than at waste in general. The total is about 0.4 kg per pupil per day, which gives the school a figure to compare against next term. None of this was visible before the weighing. Measuring changes what can be done because you cannot manage what you have not measured. Without the figures, 'we produce too much waste' is a complaint; with them it becomes a target - compost the 4.2 kg, cut the sachets, re-measure in a month and see whether it worked.
- **Q14** (3 marks) The organic waste should go into a compost pit or heap in layers: a layer of green material such as food scraps and vegetable trimmings, alternating with a layer of dry material such as dry leaves, straw or shredded paper, and turned over every week or two. Two conditions: it must be kept moist but not waterlogged, because the micro-organisms and detritivores doing the rotting need water and cannot work in dry material; and it must have air, which is why it is turned over and why the dry material is layered in to hold the heap open instead of letting it collapse into a slimy, airless, smelly mass. Given both, the heap heats up and the material breaks down into dark crumbly humus in a few months, which the school can dig into its garden.
- **Q15** (3 marks) Any two, each with a difficulty. Sell or provide water in cups or from a dispenser instead of sachets, so that no plastic is produced at all - the difficulty is that this needs a clean water supply on site, cups that have to be washed, and someone to manage it. Ask pupils to bring a refillable bottle and install a refill point - the difficulty is that pupils forget the bottle, and some families cannot afford one. Collect the sachets for recycling - the difficulty is that sachet film is of low value and hard to recycle, so a collector must be found and paid or the scheme collapses. Ban sachets on the premises - the difficulty is enforcement, and the waste may simply move outside the gate.

## EXAMINER NOTES

- Pitched at the compulsory diagram question of BECE Paper 2: 76% of the marks are at Apply level or above and 40% are Challenging.
- Q7 on why reduce beats recycle is the intellectual centre of 16.3, and it is the question pupils are least prepared for because every poster they have seen says 'reduce, reuse, recycle' in that order without saying why. The answer is that recycling is not free: collection, transport, sorting and reprocessing all cost energy, and the material degrades each time round. Reducing means none of that was ever spent.
- Q4 on the fly is the best question in 16.2. Pupils assume waste harms you by contact. It mostly does not - it harms you because something carries it. Once they see the chain (dump, flies, food, gut), the whole of sanitation makes sense, and so does the fact that a pit latrine is a waste-management measure rather than a building.
- Q10 on the needle versus the food scrap is deliberately extreme so that the principle shows: the more dangerous the waste, the further it must be kept from people, water and food. That single sentence answers every question in 16.4.
- The waste audit is the most useful practical in the whole strand and the one a school can most easily repeat. You need gloves, tongs, a spring balance or kitchen scales, and a tarpaulin or concrete area to sort on. Brief the class hard beforehand about sharp and medical waste: the rule is stop, do not touch, call the teacher.
- Weighing is what turns this from a tidy-up into data. If you have only one set of scales, weigh each category in turn as the pile is sorted rather than trying to weigh five piles at once.
- Repeat the audit a term later, after whatever changes the class decided on. A number that goes down is worth more to pupils than any poster.
